In neuroscience, researchers use computer models to comprehend complex biological processes. These models, often based on individual animal models, involve analyzing brain signal data recorded over various timescales. For our project, we applied machine learning techniques to study neuronal activity in the C. Elegans round worm, using experimental results that showcase different types of neural fluctuations. To this end, we compared the effectiveness of three time-series regression models - a linear model, an RNN model, and an RNN model with LSTM correction - on C. Elegans data. Our findings, based on nearly 1.5 million simulated C. Elegans scenarios with multiple connected neurons, suggest that RNN models accurately replicate long-term neuronal behavior while demonstrating a high degree of portability, or ability to generalize, between different neural systems. These results demonstrate that neural machine learning methods can accurately analyze brain signal data, and provide valuable insights into the underlying neural mechanisms. Our study further reveals that as the duration of observed neural fluctuations decreases, the necessary data becomes increasingly difficult to generalize from. Ultimately, we discuss the practical implications of our findings and how they are relevant to studying C. Elegans and other neural systems. Two ice models, one with crystal-like properties and another with a glassy structure, were designed to mimic distinct behaviors observed in real-world oxygen-depleted (anoxic) ices. Researchers simulated the interplay between water molecules, represented by oxygen and hydrogen atoms, and found that the glassy model effectively replicates experimental phenomena, such as the suppression of hydrogen bond asymmetry and the decrease in a water molecule's surrounding neighbors. Notably, the simulated ice exhibits a first-order transition between a stable glass phase and a metastable crystal-like phase when thermally stimulated, resulting in the formation of heterogeneously heated areas within the glassy structure. This development of crystal-glass domains signified a phase separation event, and further analysis through computational microscopy revealed patterns consistent with a hexagonal crystal arrangement in these specific areas. The presence of these crystal-glass domains was found to be observable at temperatures as low as 127 K, well below the previously estimated onset temperature of crystallization (150 K). It's also worth noting that, similar to observations in real-world anoxic ices, the simulated ice exhibited distinct layers or stratification of hydrogen atoms. These findings suggest that the distinct behaviors observed in real-world anoxic ices could be attributed to the existence of crystal-glass domains and stratified hydrogen arrangements within a water substance. This water substance, referred to as $i$-II, was previously hypothesized to possess a glassy structure. The discovery of crystal-glass domains and two-part atom arrangements provides new insights that potentially reconcile existing experimental data on anoxic ices and inspire new investigations. A significant advantage of the Scanning Tunnelling Microscope (STM) method lies in its ability to measure locally the Density Of Features (DOF) on a surface. This parameter represents the probability distribution of the surface being explored as it transitions from states with features to those without, relative to an energy threshold. Using a Titan Lytle mode STM, our research employed a series of image processing techniques to isolate and analyze the features of three different surfaces: n-type silicon, gold, and graphite. By incorporating a patch recognition algorithm to eliminate artefacts, we derived the probability distribution of the edges of the respective surface patterns from each material. These findings were then compared to the relevant theoretical models. Notably, our results for the gold and silicon surfaces align well with the expectations, while the experiments on graphite appear to be inconclusive. Ultimately, this research establishes a crucial groundwork for measuring the DOF on various materials using an STM instrument. This study also highlights the importance of utilizing an automated algorithm to remove artefacts that arise during data collection. It showcases a cost-effective and efficient image processing methodology that can be applied to a typical Lytle mode STM to derive the DOF of a material. This method involves a series of steps including ring removal, to increase the resolution of the data, and a lower threshold to isolate the probability distribution of the edges. This adapted protocol can serve as a model for measuring the DOF on scanning microscopes with similar specifications. Moreover, our experiments provide valuable insights into the nature of the probability distribution of the edges on different materials, offering a new perspective on understanding these surface characteristics. It also highlights a notable discrepancy in the probability distribution of the edges on different materials, with our results for the gold and silicon surfaces being distinctly single-peaked in contrast to the double-peaked nature observed in the experiments on graphite. This study suggests that the probability distribution of the edges on graphite may hold the key to resolving this discrepancy. It raises a variety of further questions and potential solutions, with the possibility of the observed discrepancy being a result of the method employed to derive the probability distribution. Conversely, it is also possible that the nature of the probability distribution itself varies significantly across different materials. To address this uncertainty, our research recommends exploring different imaging conditions and feature sizes in order to derive a more comprehensive understanding of the probability distribution. Text data of any length can be represented as a point in a space with an infinite number of dimensions. When the dimensionality exceeds the threshold of the data set size, it becomes impossible to store these data points in memory. Consequently, linearly independent components of the data are discarded before dimensionality reduction can be performed using techniques. However, this discarding of data components leads to a loss of information, particularly key patterns, that are essential for accurate classification, when the data is compressed using methods such as PCA. Our proposed method, on the other hand, makes it possible to represent the data without losing any of its components, and we have successfully tested its efficacy across different datasets. Our approach represents text data as node positions in a construction created by the iteratively amalgamation of clusters. When compared across 33 different datasets, it has been observed that our method consistently performs better or on par with the existing benchmark approaches. Furthermore, the preservation of all data components has resulted in retained key patterns, and we have successfully tested this phenomenon across the data sets. Our approach has also been evaluated on the problem of text summarization and our method has outperformed several state-of-the-art baselines in few-shot learning settings. Superconducting qubit performance is greatly impacted by microwave loss in its environment.  Understanding the dielectric loss plays a crucial role in achieving higher qubit frequencies, which is essential for achieving larger maximum coherence times.  We used two distinct methods to measure the dielectric loss of sapphire, a common material in superconducting qubit architectures, by first examining the dielectric loss of a sapphire sample in a inductively coupled resonator, and found the loss tangent at 4.5 GHz to be approximately 9.5 x 10^-12 when the temperature was below 80 millichelons.  We then used this knowledge to develop an experimental limit on the dielectric loss of high-purity sapphire with a frequency of 4.85 GHz, achieving an unprecedented dielectric loss of approximately 2.9 x 10^-13 when the temperature was below 80 millichelons, and setting new record for achievement of this metric. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted a visual analysis of 3 distinct datasets comprised of spatial probability distributions. Our results indicate that the multi-scale methodology provides a comprehensive framework for an extensive and nuanced analysis of the inherent structures present within complex data sets. Our approach's ability to engage with and make sense of the vast amounts of information it contains positions it as an invaluable tool within the realm of architectural design. To further solidify its potential, our research also delves into the broader implications of our approach, highlighting its adaptability and the various applications it may have within other related fields. Deep learning models' success in graph spaces is further enhanced by graph neural networks (GNNs). In contrast to their traditional machine learning counterparts, GNNs' superiority over feature engineering lies in their ability to learn and adapt from a vast amount of data. Recent advancements involve the incorporation of transfer learning, utilizing knowledge gained from one or more source domains to aid in learning another domain. Despite its widespread adoption in computer vision and natural language processing, transfer learning research for graph domains remains relatively underdeveloped. This study delves into the application of transfer learning in GNNs. We introduce a theoretical framework for formalizing transfer learning in graph context and investigate various configurations of transfer learning. To advance this field, we create an open-source dataset called CMDFP, comprising financial statements, and develop a multi-layer perceptron based model that can handle multiple source domains. Through experimental analysis, we evaluate the impact of mixing and merging source domains, as well as the challenges posed by domain overlap. The findings suggest promising directions for future research on transfer learning in graph domain. A new machine learning task called collaborative feature allocation is defined, where a constraint-based approach optimizes both feature assignments and their associated values for distinct entities, typically users and items. The goal is to develop a recommender system using data from user-item ratings, but without relying on explicit ratings, relying solely on implicit feedback in the form of binary ratings. The solution involves formulating a constrained optimization problem and using an iterative approach to develop a recommendation model. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated by several experiments, including baseline comparisons and ratings predictions on various datasets. The results indicate that this method achieves comparable or superior results compared to established models such as collaborative filtering, robust PCA, and various forms of singular value decomposition, including global and local approaches. The precision of the predictions ranged from 0.718 to 0.885, exceeding that of the baseline models in several cases. The novelty of this approach lies in the joint optimization of user-item mappings and their associated values, leading to more accurate predictions by preserving the uniqueness of the mappings. Additionally, the method allows for the discovery of latent user and item groups, making results more interpretable. The research highlights the potential of this method as a viable alternative to established recommender systems and provides avenues for further research, including the exploration of any significant biases in the obtained predictions. The research shows that this method produces fewer biases compared to the baseline models, indicating a bright future for collaborative feature allocation in the field of recommender systems. The proposed method allows for the explanation of recommendations using several metrics, such as precision, recall, and the Jaccard similarity, indicating its potential as a useful tool for explaining user-item interactions. The research shows that this method explains recommendations accurately and can be used as a valuable tool for decision-making in recommender systems. The proposed algorithm has been thoroughly tested and validated by multiple experiments, including a case study, and is available for download on GitHub under the name 'dual-cfa'. The research data and GitHub repository can be accessed via specific URLs. The research concludes by highlighting the research contributions and future directions, indicating that this method constitutes a significant innovation in the field of collaborative feature allocation. Moreover, this method represents a potential breakthrough in the field of recommender systems and can lead to future research directions, including the deepening of user-item relationships through the use of advanced algorithms. The research may also inspire the exploration of new applications of collaborative feature allocation, such as its connection to the travel recommendation problem. This tutorial outlines a specific algorithm known as Direct Transcription, which can be used to solve nonlinear systems of periodic equations. It provides an in-depth explanation of Direct Transcription and illustrates its use in a real-world design problem involving dual-patient ventilation during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our goal with this paper is to introduce Direct Transcription and facilitate its adoption in the engineering design community by making the necessary software codes accessible and incorporating them into a zipped folder within our resource repository. The primary objective of this tutorial is to facilitate understanding and implementation of Direct Transcription, which we demonstrate using a particular formulation of the dual-patient ventilation problem that highlights its complexities. The underlying problem we address involves formulating a nonlinear periodic optimization problem to develop a strategy for simultaneously ventilating two patients with inconsistent respiratory patterns. The final solution we obtain through Direct Transcription showcases the efficacy of this algorithm in obtaining accurate numerical solutions for a wide array of parameter values, and our results also shed light on various design variables and their interrelated dynamics. The tutorial's focus on parameterized solutions and their dependence on multiple design variables sets the stage for future research involving optimization, and our extensive theoretical and practical analysis demonstrates the general applicability of Direct Transcription to a broad range of engineering design problems by identifying the underlying underlying commonalities, and highlights several key research opportunities arising from the pandemic that remain largely unexplored. The codes for this project can be found in the repository below at https://github.com/fengjunwang95/Direct-Transcription-for-Dual-Patient-Ventilation. The specific implementation used here was developed using the pyProblem and pySparse frameworks within PyOM, and it would be highly recommended that the reader familiarizes themselves with this tools and their individual papers before reading this tutorial. The reader is also invited to contact the authors directly for further clarification or feedback, and the team would be more than happy to schedule a video meeting at your convenience. A rational map $f$ from the Riemann sphere to itself is bicritical if it has precisely two points where the derivative is zero. We identify the "deck clusters" for iterates of bicritical maps, consisting of points that map to a common set under repeated applications of $f$. In cases where $f$ is bicritical and non-constant, we show that there are either two, one, or no points in the pre-image of a given point under iterations of $f$. Additionally, we explore the possible sizes of such "deck clusters" and provide a descriptive framework, outlining specific classes of bicritical maps that fit particular criteria. Furthermore, we derive quantitative results regarding the sizes of "deck clusters" and establish a limit on their maximum size in relation to the degree of $f$. In cases where $f$ is bicritical and degree $d$ exceeds 2, we demonstrate that for any given point in the Riemann sphere, the number of pre-images under repeated applications of $f$ is bounded by $2\lceil (d-1)/2 \rceil$. A major challenge in the general continuum-limit thermodynamic mixture theory for multi-component gas mixtures arises from the need to solve a complex nonlinear problem that requires efficient iteration to converge. According to the Boltzmann equation, this iteration can be very computationally expensive. Nevertheless, researchers have discovered that under specific conditions in the rarefied regime, a simplified version of the stream problem allows for the separation of complex nonlinear factors, significantly reducing computational load. In this study, the researchers further develop these concepts by creating a numerical method to address the issues in the mixture theory. They demonstrate that their approach can significantly improve computational efficiency while maintaining accurate results. Furthermore, by creating tools that take advantage of a simplification in the stream problem, they are able to reduce the number of iterations needed for convergence in the stream solution itself. All of these methods were tested in realistic simulations of gas mixtures flowing through a channel and around a sphere, showing reliable consistency with simulation results in the continuum limit as well as with simulation results from a direct solution of the Boltzmann equation in the rarefied regime. All of the methods were shown to be computationally efficient, converging in a dozen iterations or less in realistic simulations. Interestingly, the tools developed for the stream solution were found to be applicable even in the direct simulation of the full fluid. In addition to these methods for the stream solution, the researchers also developed a numerical method to address the thermalization of the gas mixture. Since thermalization requires a significant amount of thermal energy, a simplification of the thermal solution from the Boltzmann equation was not available. As such, the numerical method developed for thermalization does not take advantage of a simplification in the thermal solution itself. However, through testing in various realistic simulations of gas mixtures flowing through a channel and around a simple geometric shape, the researchers were able to show that their method for thermalization is efficient and reliable in the continuum limit as well as in the rarefied regime. Notably, the computational load for thermalization was found to be similar to the load for the stream solution in the rarefied regime. These new methods for efficient solution of the general continuum-limit multiscale gas flow problem were found to be reliable and computationally practical. In particular, the efficiency of the methods was found to be similar to the efficiency of the stream solution in the rarefied regime and significantly better than in the full fluid regime. In addition to these methods for efficient solution of the gas flow problem, the researchers also developed a numerical method for thermalization

The primary objective of x-ray optics is to effectively concentrate x-ray energy while minimizing losses due to a phenomenon called grazing incidence. A key aspect of this is achieving the precise focusing required for x-ray instruments, given the narrow beam width at the point of grazing incidence. This inherently increases the complexity of designing optical systems for tasks like imaging, particularly for those requiring wide-field coverage. In this study, we explore different approaches to achieve a required beam width, focusing on a type of x-ray lens known as multi-layer technology. By using segmented, multi-layered optics that incorporate various design features - such as different curvature radii, offsetting feature orientations, and curved outer surfaces - our calculations determine the feasibility of these designs for wide-field x-ray applications. A notable advantage of these enhanced optical designs is their potential to be used in a type of x-ray imaging device known as a wide-field polar emission lens, offering a means to concentrate x-rays while maintaining a large capture angle. A major benefit of this device is its ability to serve as both a concentrated beam source for x-ray scattering applications and a wide-field imaging tool when the device itself is imaged. By combining the optical design with an imaging technique known as pixelated microcalorimeter, our studies demonstrate the feasibility of achieving a wide field of view, a high spatial resolution, and a high signal-to-noise ratio - a combination that could significantly advance x-ray astronomy and imaging, and potentially lead to new fields of study such as x-ray timing and multi-messenger astronomy. This work highlights the importance of both focusing and imaging optical designs for x-ray applications, and how these techniques could be used to inform other fields of study. A key example of this is the potential for near future x-ray telescopes to serve as highly sensitive detectors of gravitational waves, by using the existing x-ray optical design in a novel way to detect these waves. By exploring this potential, our studies demonstrate the significance of interdisciplinary research and the potential for x-ray optical design to inform discoveries in this rapidly evolving field. Researchers commonly utilize synthetic control algorithms, a method involving a weighted average of past time period data to create a control group comparable to treatment group. The efficacy of these weights is typically evaluated using goodness-of-fit metrics. We argue that this approach is inadequate because it's centered around non-causal, non-identifiable estimates of the treated unit's potential outcomes. We propose an alternative method focused on a nearby causal version of the model, allowing for the estimation of counterfactuals for treated and control units near their pre-treatment values. Our novel method yields a new object of study, leading to improved goodness-of-fit measures that facilitate efficient optimization of the synthetic control algorithm. We demonstrate the success of this method by applying it to four case studies. Moreover, we connect our results to two proprietary databases: the Consumption Expenditure Data and the Quantitative Easing Program Data. We publicly release our Python code at github.com/jayfodge/synthetic_control. We also build upon and expand upon a 2020 paper by Colombo and Ponomareva.

This presents a challenge in selecting the most suitable images for a given subject, as changing the lighting or background can noticeably alter the object's appearance. To address this issue, we've developed a method that accurately replicates image effects while preserving the object's original appearance, by creating a master image with optimal lighting and a neutral background through minimal image manipulation. Our proposed pipeline involves training a deep neural network model to transfer styles between images, as well as a new optimization algorithm to find a solution that meets multiple objectives without altering the image content. We've also designed a user interface to interactively specify color targets through brushstrokes, allowing for multiple color effects to be achieved from a single input. Our method was tested on various image collections and demonstrated the ability to create a range of compelling color styles by repurposing a single master image. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of creating a diverse set of images from a single object using our method, including a video showcase at https://vimeo.com/187657013. Our source code is available at https://github.com/lethray/crime. We publicly demonstrate the method at https://crosscamera.netlify.com/, showcasing a range of crime scene-inspired applications. The Transit Feed Specification (TFS) enables efficient real-time data exchange between transit operators and information display systems, allowing coordination and standardized information presentation. TFS is widely used in North America, and its main advantage is providing updated transit information as feeds and updates. Despite this efficiency, drawing TFS maps and overlaying routes and stops on a map in real-time requires additional processing and can be time-consuming. This extra processing is particularly tedious during events or construction that affect transit routes, as it often requires manual adjustment in feed specifications to turn off unwanted routes and labels. This problem can be efficiently countered by applying a Recurrent Neural Network that generates a TFS feed indicating which routes and stops are affected by events or construction, and at what time they take effect or end. This TFS feed can then be used by operators to easily modify the feed and overlay a updated map in real-time. This solution was implemented and demonstrated by Hebrew University of Jerusalem Public Transportation Information System during the ITT@Intertraffic 2019 exhibition in Amsterdam. This paper presents a short-term TFS feed prediction model based on a specific condition, and demonstrates its success by presenting experimental validation results. The proposed model is particularly useful for dynamic information such as events and construction that are typically handled manually due to changing schedules and times. This model is particularly beneficial for large public transit systems as it saves time and resources by automating TFS feed processing for these type of information. The proposed model has a particular success in handling multiple type of information while taking into consideration possible invalid outputs. The developed code is also presented as it is currently implemented in an open-source Python project. The project utilizes the TFS2API library for efficient TFS feed processing and processing of derived information such as routes and stops. The base model is also available as a open-source, standalone, Recurrent Neural Network model in the TensorFlow community. This issue is particularly complex when dealing with categories characterized by subtle attributes and diverse negative examples. In response, we introduce a novel approach that learns prototypes based on common characteristics shared among a class type, as opposed to traditional methods that focus on individual categories. This strategy enables us to achieve better generalization by mitigating the impact of negative data and promoting invariant traits. Our framework not only accurately identifies key attributes but also accommodates diverse forms of data representation, allowing for effective classification. Extensive experiments have demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed method, and we have successfully applied it to various benchmark datasets with impressive results. Ground-and-air sensor networks (GASNs) integrate sensors and sensors on the ground and airborne vehicles. Each ground station connects with a central control station via a satellite or airborne plane through a wireless link. In this study, we investigate the formation of a gasyn link, where a ground station links with an airborne vehicle, as a stochastic process. Initially, each ground station and airborne plane lists their preferred connections in order of priority. Then, each ground plane prioritizes its connections with ground stations in a specific order. Next, a ground plane determines its link priorities with ground stations based on signal strength and distance. Gasyn links are established through a prioritized process, where each ground station and airborne vehicle strive to establish their top priority connections. We develop three models for this process, where each model differs in its update rule for link establishment. These models are: modified last-come-first-served (MLCFS), constant time (CT), and random time (RT). In the RT model, ground stations and airborne vehicles update their links immediately once priorities change. However, ground stations update their links only when they receive a update from a ground plane, where the model becomes constant time. Each model is studied as a discrete-time Markov chain, where the model's state represents the link connections between ground stations and airborne vehicles. In the model's analysis, the model's state transition probabilities are found to depend on the network's topology and the change in link connections. Ground station analysis reveals that the likelihood of a link change between ground stations and airborne vehicles decreases exponentially, where the link change is driven by changes in signal strength. Furthermore, the model's stability, where the link connections between ground stations and airborne vehicles, remain unchanged, is shown to depend on the network's topology and the signal strength between ground stations and airborne vehicles. By assuming that ground stations and airborne vehicles update their links continuously, we study a continuous-time Markov process for the model. In the model's analysis, the model's state transition rates were derived as linear functions of signal strength. Through numerical analysis, the model's properties were studied as a discrete-time Markov chain. In the model's numerical analysis, the model's state transition probabilities were graphed as a function of signal strength and the change in link connections. In the model's numerical analysis, the model's results were verified using network simulator. In the model's validation, the model's results were compared with actual data, where the model's results were shown to be comparable to actual data for various signal strengths.

We've developed an advanced technique for identifying topological features in collider data by combining multiple tagger algorithms. We've demonstrated through detached analyses the efficacy of our method by assessing the reliability of single and merged top tagger algorithms in detecting either a top quark jet or a top quark in association with a W boson. By calculating Shapley values, which utilize Bayesian inference, we've determined the probability of each tagger emitting event data that would identify a top quark jet or a top quark W boson junction at their respective optimal thresholds. This technique allows us, along with existing information theory methods, to analyze and interpret the performance of our top tagging procedure. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the ability of our method to be used as a machine learning model in the future. We also analyze how the combination of top taggers performs when trained on simulated data featuring intercorrelated signals and backgrounds. We found that our interpretation method is effective in simplied scenarios but encounters difficulties in understanding the performance of our algorithm in the presence of correlations between signals and backgrounds. To overcome this challenge, we extended Shapley values to a variant called Shapley values for conditional expectation values. We successfully applied this modified approach to a complex case and were able to determine the probabilities of our top tagging procedure producing incorrect results for specific event types. We found that our original interpretation method is effective in most cases but may require this modified approach in situations of complex dependency between signals and backgrounds. We have also developed a new technique for identifying topological features by training our merged top taggers on simulated data featuring top quark s-channels both with and without jets. Through multiple rounds of training and refitting, we discovered a merged top tagger that demonstrates improved performance in identifying top quark jets by a factor of approximately five compared to a single top tagger and to top quark identification algorithms. We have further optimized multiple top taggers for identifying top quark W boson junctions in association with jets. We found that these optimized merged top taggers possess higher discrimination capabilities for identifying top quark W boson junctions at the LHC. We were able to determine that a top quark W boson signal can be identified at 75% reliability with approximately 80% reliability in identifying contaminating top quark jets. We were able to achieve this level of optimization for both a top quark W boson tagger and a top quark jet tagger by leveraging our advanced algorithm. We were able to successfully test and apply multiple top taggers

Using experience replay in policy gradient methods, such as policy iteration and policy search, has been shown to improve performance by combining multiple policies. However, replaying all past experiences can slow down optimization due to outdated information, and limiting the experiences to current iterations only disregards previously acquired knowledge. A novel replay mechanism, named Variance Diminishing Experience Replay (VDER), has been proposed to efficiently utilize past experiences. VDER assigns a variable variance factor to each experience pool, updated after each iteration, which balances the frequency of replaying recent and older experiences. A small variance factor indicates a higher likelihood of replaying older experiences, whereas a large variance factor indicates a higher likelihood of replaying more recent experiences. As the variance factor adapts to the iteration number, VDER optimizes performance by leveraging the benefits of older and newer experiences. Moreover, VDER introduces a uniform distribution of past and present policies within the experience pool to boost exploration and ensure that the policy gradient estimator remains unbiased. The proposed VDER is evaluated using real-world games, such as chess and shogi, and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing replay methods including uniform sampling, recent-experience replay, and prior-experience replay. The VDER approach is further theoretical justification for its performance has been established. In particular, a proven upper bound of the estimated action-value function based on VDER is established using the Bellman equation, which is used to derive a global, gradient-free optimization algorithm similar to policy iteration, but with improved convergence. The proposed VDER is evaluated and compared to several recent policy gradient methods across real-world games and benchmark suites. The performance of VDER highlights its effectiveness in minimizing variance through experience adaptation and its resulting local convexification, ultimately leading to improved empirical and theoretical performance. In the context of functional integrals, specifically Gaussian integrals, a recent publication introduced the superbosonization equation, and a new investigation confirms that it is equivalent to the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation in the manner described in the literature. Furthermore, it is shown that these two methods yield the same result when applied to the specific scenario of four-dimensional supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. While the superbosonization equation appears to be a more convenient formula, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is presented as a more comprehensive method. A step-by-step demonstration of the proof is provided to facilitate understanding. The process involves expressing the supersymmetric Yang-Mills functional integral in the form of a Gaussian integral through the introduction of fermionic and bosonic matrix components. Subsequently, applying the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation yields an expression in terms of supersymmetric path integrals of fermionic and bosonic Yang-Mills theories with appropriate coupling constants. An alternative approach utilizes the superbosonization equation with a parameter $s$, and taking the limit as $s$ approaches 1/4 results in the desired supersymmetric Yang-Mills functional integral. An accompanying discussion explores the application of these methods in the context of Yang-Mills theory at all dimensions and discusses the process of supersymmetry enhancement via the relevant path integrals. A related work presents a new understanding of the relationship between Yang-Mills theories of different dimensions, specifically that supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory in four dimensions efficiently reduces to Yang-Mills theory in three dimensions when the Chern-Simons term is incorporated. While researchers have made significant progress in NLP through word-level modeling, a parallel advancement in computer vision has been achieved through motion extension. This involves extending static images to include dynamic information, leading to more accurate and detailed outcomes in applications such as image forecasting and video classification. This has resulted in improved performance across a range of tasks. However, the current method of motion enhancement in models like RNN and RNN derivatives has been found to suffer from several issues. For instance, the presence of noisy data, like outliers and covariates, can adversely affect predictive models. Furthermore, the memory and output from recurrent models are often entangled, leading to information loss. Also, the linear progression in linear models can be a limitation. This research develops new techniques to counter these challenges and presents new methods for learning both static and dynamic features simultaneously. Experiments conducted on both artificial datasets and real-world applications demonstrate the efficacy of these methods for detailed predictive modeling. For example, the success of the method in detecting DDooS attacks while filtering out false positives highlights its potential in handling intricate learning tasks across a range of domains. Also, the method's performance in forecasting patterns while filtering out noisy data and information that is not relevant for real-world scenarios. This research validates the usefulness of detailed feature learning in real-world applications and opens up possibilities for further exploration in model development. For instance, the possibility of utilizing the power of ensembles in ensemble detail learning is a promising area for advancement. For comprehensive details, please refer to our scientific article published in https://arxiv.org/submit/ or the associated code repository at https://github.com/quantric/moldernn to gain insights into the utility of the method in real-time learning across a range of computer vision tasks. Additionally, the accompanying paper details our research in model development for applications such as anomaly detection, DDooS attack prediction, and image forecasting based on the impact of information loss in real-time scenarios. Ultimately, the method has far-reaching implications for model development in a variety of domains including image classification, object detection, and image generation. We examine the Point Spread Functions (PSFs) of various image combinations from disparate libraries of unrelated images. Our research reveals that the PSFs of minima and maxima in combined images are particularly sensitive to interferences resulting from overlapping galaxy centers and the background in individual images. Moreover, the PSFs of double galaxy pairs exhibit distinct characteristics based on the orientation and position of the observed galaxy units. These findings form the basis for a method to automatically identify double galaxy pairs by analyzing the variations in combined image PSFs. This technique holds significant potential for validation and complementarity with parameter estimation methods for event time-delay. Its potential applicability also encompasses situations where single galaxy images are not resolvable. Our work further involves an analytical model for calculating the PSFs of combined images, primarily focusing on the influence of the galaxy luminosity distribution. Although this model is primarily numerical, it can be used analytically to derive closed-form expressions under the assumption of a Gaussian or Cauchy probability distribution for the individual galaxy positions. Notably, the derived expressions accurately describe the combined PSF behavior at low signal-to-noise ratios. Our research also demonstrates that the PSFs of steady-state light sources in a steady state are unaffected by alterations in the steady state. To prevent false positives, our proposed verification method for validation and complementarity must therefore exclude steady states that encompass multiple galaxy components. Moreover, the PSFs of combined images derived from galaxies with or without shared centers differ significantly, and our approach must consequently distinguish between these two cases. Finally, the effectiveness and reliability of our proposed proposed approach were assessed through numerical simulations of various configurations. The resulting correlation coefficients between simulated and estimated values of the PSFs range from 0.85 to 0.99. The accuracy of our estimates appears to be influenced by the precision of the input data, and future studies should aim to expand the understanding of our approach's applicability by considering additional configurations. The underlying algorithms and software used in this research have been made publicly available for the purpose of independent verification and implementation. A detailed user manual outlining the necessary steps for employing our method has been provided. Specifically, the research team has identified and addressed five key challenges associated with deriving and analyzing the PSFs of combined images, and proposed solutions to address these complexities. The derived algorithms and codes hold significant potential for advancing the field of gravitational lens modeling and modeling gravitational lenses. Artificial neural networks have been used in cell research to analyze the complex interactions between genetic, biochemical, and physical cellular systems (cellular morphology) at various scales. They have also been employed to study the development of cells (embryogenesis) and the impact of diseases on cell shape (cellular pathology). In this research, we explore the use of implicit neural representations to create a new level of cell geometry, which can learn and accurately replicate the spatial structure of cells without any prior knowledge of its parts. By combining a latent vector representation and a signed graph learning method that identifies causal relationships, we have developed a novel framework for understanding cell morphology without any prior expertise. Through experiments using interactive 3D cell visualizations, we have successfully demonstrated our ability to analyze cell shapes, generate new cells, identify cells that are similar, and modify existing cells to mimic diseases like muscular sarcotubular myopathy. Our model and associated code are openly available for further research and development. In particular, we have made significant strides in generating quasi-realistic 3D cellular structures using signed graph-based diffusion models, which hold promise for a wider range of applications. Our results and findings have important implications for cellular and molecular biology, and we expect this work to open up new avenues for modeling and simulating cell growth and development. In this research, we have also tackled two high-level challenges in biology using neural networks. First, we have successfully discovered the underlying causal structure of embryogenesis in mouse embryos using graph neural networks. Second, we have identified a quantitative model of cellular pathology in humans by combining multiple lines of evidence, including clinical descriptions, genetic mutations, and protein dysfunction. Our results demonstrate the power of neural networks in discovering and validating biological insights. In summary, we have employed neural networks to extract valuable information about the spatial structure of cells, its causal relationships, and various biological processes such as embryogenesis and cellular pathology. Blind, low-vision, and print-impaired individuals still struggle with accessing standard document formats like PDF, due to a lack of suitable descriptions and navigation capabilities. In particular, documents often lack such descriptions, making it difficult for assistive technology to understand their structure. As a result, users are forced to rely on redundant information within the content itself, which often leads to significant reading difficulties and fatigue. In this study, we underscore the importance of document navigability for print-impaired individuals and identify key requirements for creating a navigable electronic document. Essential attributes of a navigable document include the ability to identify and access individual items such as headings, subheadings, images, and tables, as well as related alt-text descriptions. To achieve this goal, we propose modifying the existing TOC (Table of Contents) concept and incorporating SAI (Scene And Description) alt-text, which combines visual descriptions with related textual content. By implementing these innovative concepts, we aim to significantly improve the accessibility of standard documents for print-impaired individuals, thereby enhancing their overall quality of life. Two proof-of-concept demos were developed in collaboration with print-impaired individuals to validate the identified requirements. An accessible document is envisioned as a TOC-enabled content that provides SAI descriptions for users, thereby simplifying navigation and enabling print-impaired individuals to access and engage with standard documents. This work is part of a larger project, the Accessible Content Across Borders (ACAB) initiative, aimed at developing a universal standard for creating accessible digital content across cultures and regions. As part of this effort, we conducted extensive research involving print-impaired participants from five countries, observing them using assistive technologies to read PDFs. Notably, two of our participants were experts who had shared their knowledge on accessibility best practices through public presentations and social media, yet they continued to struggle with accessing standard document formats. Through our research, we identified the need for print-impaired individuals to repetitively ask for unsolicited feedback and suggestions on accessibility as a form of politeness and cultural norm. To address these social norms, we discovered that print-impaired individuals require accessible information about the content itself, creating a need for consistent metadata that describes the structure and availability of accessible elements within a document. As a result, we propose the Navigators social network platform, a central hub for print-impaired individuals to connect with others and share knowledge and resources related to accessibility. By building this platform, we aim to create a community around accessibility, promoting cultural and behavioral changes that prioritize accessibility

The ultimate goal of our project is to develop high-performance simulation models capable of efficiently predicting the dispersal of disperse objects moving through the atmosphere and within the ocean following an asteroid impact.  Key factors influencing disperse element dispersal include gravitational forces, the composition of the material being ejected, and the presence of atmospheric drag.  To address this complex scenario, we are implementing multiple numerical modeling approaches, including a bespoke code, ASTER, whose atmospheric simulation model origins date back to the Sixties, in addition to utilizing the open-source software CLAWPACK.  Furthermore, we are leveraging a novel finite-volume-based solver known as FLAW, which is currently under development as a Python-based CLAW utility, and the state-of-the-art software CLAW252D, a 252-dimensional solver developed by Bryan Bazzell.  To account for variable drag forces affecting the disperse objects as they move through the atmosphere, we are implementing a dynamic adaptation technique, which involves utilizing a range of control functions, including a logarithmic scale, to efficiently reduce the spatial and temporal resolution where necessary.  Adaptation is controlled by a measure of the solution's magnitude relative to the specified control function.  Our approaches are tested with a range of benchmark experiments, including an experimental simulation replicating the famous Chelyabinsk asteroid's atmospheric entry in 2013 and a simulation of dispersal within both the ocean and atmosphere following an asteroid impact.  Key outcomes from these numerical modeling experiments are presented in terms of the final spatial distribution of the disperse objects at the conclusion of the simulation.  Specifically, the solutions generated using the dynamic adaptation technique are compared to a reference solution generated using a standard finite-volume approach with predetermined spatial and temporal resolution parameters.  Our adaptation-based simulation results indicate that the technique leads to a significant reduction in computational cost while maintaining accuracy relative to the reference solution.  Specifically, the results demonstrate that the technique allows for a 1/1000th reduction in temporal resolution and 1/100th reduction in spatial resolution while still accurately capturing the final spatial distribution of the disperse objects.  One potential area for further research to refine the adaptation technique involves investigating a variant of the method that incorporates a control function accounting for the object's size, which could potentially yield an additional order of magnitude reduction in computational cost.  Our proposed approach to adapting the solution in this manner is informed by the significant impact that the object's size has on its growth rate as it progresses through the atmosphere. Variations in the precipitation patterns worldwide are primarily driven by different types of El Ni\~no events, which have distinct geographical and seasonal impacts.  Our research focuses on two major forms of El Ni\~no - the Central Pacific and the Eastern Pacific - each characterized by distinct climate and weather anomalies.  By examining global rainfall trends in relation to these two types of El Ni\~no events, particularly during cooler and warmer periods, we identified significant disparities in precipitation amounts and seasonal distributions.  For example, the Central Pacific El Ni\~no events tend to have lower total rainfall but higher seasonal variability, more frequent droughts in cooler months, and reduced precipitation during the summer.  By contrast, the Eastern Pacific events have higher total rainfall but less seasonal variation, less summer droughts, and greater summer precipitation.  These findings underscore the importance of distinguishing between the two unique forms of El Ni\~no events when studying climate variability and change, particularly in forecasting global rainfall.  Such distinctions may reveal new insights into the links between climate and weather systems and help predict the consequences of future climate shifts.  For instance, regions like East Africa and Australia, which experience most of their rainfall during the summer, are particularly vulnerable to variations in the frequency and intensity of Eastern Pacific El Ni\~no events.  By contrast, regions like southern Chile and Colombia, which receive the majority of their precipitation during the winter, are more susceptible to changes in the Central Pacific El Ni\~no events.  These potential climate risks highlight the need for a better understanding of the unique characteristics of El Ni\~no events and their differential impacts on global rainfall patterns and the world's most critical climate regions.  By combining statistical and dynamical modeling with extensive observations of precipitation and temperature, our research aims to improve our knowledge of the links between climate and weather conditions worldwide and support data-driven policy decisions in countries most affected by these global climate variability and change.  The distinctions between the two types of El Ni\~no events and their impacts also imply the necessity of developing new metrics to capture their distinct geographical and seasonal impacts on global rainfall and help predict the differential effects of future climate shifts.  Such efforts may also shed more light on the links between climate and weather systems and their implications for a better prediction of climate variability and change.  By studying the unique features of Eastern and Central Pacific El Ni\~no events and their impacts worldwide, our research contributes to a more accurate understanding of the global consequences of future climate shifts. Cyber-Physical Systems, particularly those with high functionality demands, often require enhanced resilience capabilities to guarantee timely system shutdown and reinitiation within critical performance thresholds when faced with catastrophic component failures. This study proposes a resilience framework for CPSs, governed by specifications that utilize temporal logic to define and efficiently manage the desired level of system continuity in the face of component failures. This framework incorporates algorithms for assessing resilience costs, evaluating and validating resilience strategies, and implementing the most suitable approach in multi-viewpoint scenarios. The study's effectiveness is demonstrated through the examination of a case study involving a dynamic pattern-based CPS. This research offers a theoretical foundation for evaluating and assessing various resilience strategies in CPSs, which can be utilized in the design of future CPSs and the improvement of existing systems. The presented approach has been successfully validated in practical environments. 

Key aspects of this research:
- A theoretical framework for CPS resilience has been introduced, focusing on specifications governed by temporal logic.
- The study introduces algorithms for evaluating and validating resilience strategies in multi-viewpoint scenarios.
- The RML language and EMF-based implementation of STL specifications have been leveraged to assess and compare resilience strategies in CPSs.
- The study introduces a formal framework for evaluating multiple resilience strategies in CPSs and identifying the most suitable approach based on predefined criteria such as cost, timing, and others.

For decades, scientists have been searching for "dark matter," a theoretical particle that doesn't interact with light but affects space gravity, without success. To improve these searches, a new method is proposed to detect this matter by using large-scale networks of accelerometers, similar to gravity sensors, at mineral deposits, volcanoes, and other locations with extensive underground structures. By calculating subtle changes in inter-node gravity within these networks, scientists can detect tiny gravitational variations caused by hypothetical dark matter particles. This technique has the potential to probe a previously unexplored area of mass range for these particles, and even locations with thinner underground coverage can be incorporated through advanced data analysis methods connecting multiple nodes. Although no significant detection has been reported during a 12-month experimental period with six accelerometers, this experiment has set new limits on the density of dark matter within specific radial regions around locations like the Homestake gold mine. continued to probe new areas of parameter space for dark matter, and similar experiments are planned to further explore this matter with even higher sensitivity in the coming years. Future experiments will utilize 13 underground sites with advanced deep networking around the world, and one such project at the 610-meter high Frejus tunnel in the 2022 Monte Carlo Grand Prix even has a race-inspired name: the "Rally for Dark Matter." This project aims to probe the matter at an unprecedented level of 1 femtogram/cm^3 sensitivity, and scientists are also exploring other innovative sites like the 3333-meter deep Kola Superdeep Borehole in Murmansk, Russia, with plans to lower the detection limit to a staggering 0.01 pg/cm^3 – a whopping 180 times more sensitive than the latest experiment. This race to discover even smoother underground structures and deeper depths is set to continue in the coming years. A comprehensive overview of these efforts has been presented at the 57th Symposium on Relativistic Astrophysics in innsbruck, Austria in 2019 and the 23rd International Conference on Artificial Grounded Structures in Edinburgh, Scotland in 2018, and related data have been uploaded to the repository for public access under the guidance of the theory team. Continued advances in these experiments are expected to provide new insights into the nature of dark matter. It then demonstrates that these measures can serve as time-dependent functionals of a theory's symmetry group, which in turn influences how interactions are mediated and recorded. Furthermore, these concepts may facilitate the development of new paradigms for physics and biology. We explore these ideas in the context of two examples: Bell's theorem, space-time foam, and the phenomenon of memory in pathogens. In the case of Bell's theorem, we propose a measure of nonlocality that is maximized under certain conditions. Space-time foam is used to illustrate how nonlocality can be associated with absolute space-time invariance. When a node sends its timer, nearby nodes comparing their local timers with the received value can determine their correct parental relationship. Consequently, the protocol allows nodes to self-organize a spanning tree in a distributed and efficient manner. Notably, the system avoids the need for synchronization, a challenging task to implement, and the overall process is straightforward and reliable. This paper introduces a new motion planning approach based on space partitioning for autonomous vehicles navigating dynamic environments with moving obstacles. To efficiently navigate these environments, the proposed algorithm generates discrete spatial snapshots and constructs a roadmap of low-cost paths through a hierarchy of spatial granularities. The approach starts with a high-resolution space division where the planner identifies feasible spatial movements and switches to coarser granularities when the roadmap does not improve significantly. The state-of-the-art planner, TORC, is used to solve the motion planning problem within each spatial domain. The proposed planner's ability to adapt its sampling rate and focus on critical areas with high obstacle density and low visibility contributes to its high performance. Moreover, it outperforms other planners by finding more accurate solutions. In contrast to many iron-based superconductors that exhibit nematic order and an intricate connection between their electronic properties, we have found that LiFeAs does not undergo nematic instability. Utilizing first-principles calculations, we created a model that captures the interplay between the spin-flip and d-wave antiferromagnetic interactions. Surprisingly, this model reveals a broad interval within which the d-wave interaction cannot induce nematic order. The origin of this phenomenon lies in the unique characteristics of LiFeAs's Fermi surface, particularly its absence from the time-reversal invariant momentum, where maximum susceptibility is typically observed in other materials. As a result, a normal state with higher symmetry, rather than one with nematic properties, is stabilized in LiFeAs. This finding supports experimental results indicating that LiFeAs does not become unstable under a 45-degree rotation of its lattice. Our research also shows that certain Fermi surface modifications, resulting from chemical substitution or strain, could potentially introduce nematic behavior in the system. The scenario is comparable to the situation observed in hydrazine-based superconductors, where nematic order arises from local spin nematicity on a certain type of orbital. If this analogy holds true, it would imply that the symmetry of the electronic states in LiFeAs is similar to its non-magnetic CuInP2S6 counterpart. However, further verification of this idea is required. Ultimately, our research highlights the significance of performing rigorous theoretical calculations to understand the properties of various superconductors before conducting expensive and time-consuming experiments. The model we developed in LiFeAs is unique in that it considers the interplay between spin-flip and d-wave interactions, neither of which has been extensively explored in the literature. The model also has implications for understanding the mechanisms behind iron-based superconductors and other materials with unique properties, particularly in cases where d-wave interactions may play a dominant role. The model's potential applications in these cases could provide valuable insights into their underlying physics and potentially reveal new ways to manipulate their electronic properties, leading to novel devices and applications. The possibility of introducing nematic behavior in LiFeAs through chemical substitution or strain also suggests that this material could serve as a reference point or a starting point for creating new materials with similar properties, potentially opening up new avenues for research and discovery in the field of superconductivity and materials science. We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of Global $\chi^2$ fits for four types of 2HDM, utilizing recent experimental results to evaluate various parameters. Our findings, incorporating new data from the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMBB), future colliders, and neutrino theory, reveal substantial reductions in parameter space for each of the four 2HDM types: 2HDM with Type I, II, III, and IV couplings. Specifically, inclusion of future collider results achieves: (i) an order of magnitude reduction in parameter space for Type I and II 2HDM, (ii) substantial reductions for Type III and IV 2HDM, albeit one order of magnitude lower than for Type I and II. When incorporating results from future Cosmic Microwave Background measurements, SM4 constraints at colliders, and SM4 low-energy observables, the reduced parameter space for each 2HDM type becomes nearly one order of magnitude. Future results from neutrino theory also significantly reduce parameter space for Type I, II, and IV 2HDM. However, despite current and future constraints, the possibility of encountering a global minimum beyond the SM remains plausible, especially for Type III and IV 2HDM. In contrast, for Type I and II 2HDM, the likelihood of a local SM minimum as the global minimum remains higher, albeit still a small probability. Finally, our analysis indicates that Type I, II, and IV 2HDM have the potential to meet the requirement of Global $\chi^2$ fits with naturalness, whereas Type III 2HDM falls short. Nonetheless, its naturalness could be restored should its CP symmetry prove conserved. The study supplements our prior work, complementing recent assessments of 2HDM parameter space in reports by the LHC and ILC. The research was carried out using the f2n and Global2HDM tools. In this research, we investigate the potential of evolved virtual "cells" with basic sensory capabilities to actively select and maintain advantageous cooperative strategies within a group. We compare the effectiveness of probabilistic learning and an evolutionary algorithm in a medium-sized cooperative group of agents consisting of 20 members. The results demonstrate that an evolutionary approach often yields more efficient cooperative systems compared to probabilistic selection, especially those that strategically coordinate actions to maximize impact. Furthermore, we discovered that coherent and effective cooperative systems tend to emerge from diverse populations, even overcoming challenges related to parasitic elements that exploit vulnerable systems. Additional findings indicate that cooperative systems consistently exhibit increased complexity and innovative solutions. Overall, this research highlights the capacity of artificial life simulations to uncover novel insights into cooperative strategy development. It also lays the groundwork for future investigations into the adaptive processes of evolving cooperative groups, including the evolution of self-assembling structures and the ability to address and rectify parasitic threats. We have developed a theoretical approach that considers the influence of a strongly excited vibrational mode on a nearby magnon, offering a precise description within a time-dependent magnetic framework. By applying this framework to a specific compound, yttrium iron garnet, we are able to quantify how the magnon's frequency and damping are affected when the system is heated. Additionally, we have created a mathematical description for the rate at which the magnon's energy is dissipated in terms of its nonlinear interaction with the vibrational mode. It is observed that as the magnon's energy approaches the vibrational mode's energy, the magnon's frequency and damping exhibit complex behaviors that are indicative of a phenomenon known as nonperturbative or nonlinear behavior. Moreover, we are able to provide a detailed explanation for how the magnon's frequency and damping are affected in terms of its relative energy with respect to the vibrational mode's energy. Experimental validation in the form of high-resolution magneto-optical spectroscopy reveals that as the magnon's energy approaches the vibrational mode's energy, the magnon's frequency experiences an unexpected shift known as the nonlinear spectral shift, demonstrating a positive correlation between this shift and the magnon's energy. Furthermore, we are able to provide a detailed explanation for how the nonlinear spectral shift is influenced in terms of the magnon's relative energy with respect to the vibrational mode's energy. These findings provide fundamental insight into the magnon-vibron coupling and the formation of a common quasiparticle in the low-energy spectrum, while also shedding light on the magnon's behavior in a range of energy configurations. Moreover, we are able to provide a detailed explanation for how the magnon's frequency and damping are affected in terms of the characteristics of a specific mathematical function known as the Bose-damped harmonic oscillator. The theoretical approach used in this study is a significant advancement in the field and provides a crucial foundation for understanding the magnon-vibron coupling and the formation of a shared quasiparticle in the low-energy spectrum. Moreover, it is anticipated that the findings will inspire further experimental and theoretical investigations of the magnon-vibron coupling and the low-energy spectrum in a range of antiferromagnetic materials. The theoretical framework used in this study is a versatile tool that can be applied to a wide range of energy configurations and is therefore a valuable resource for understanding the magnon-vibron coupling and the low-energy spectrum in a variety of situations. This research introduces two alterations for Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem.
Originally utilizing the Griesmer code, Loidreau's system has limited parameters,
resulting in relatively weak security. To improve this, we suggest two changes.
First, we recommend selecting from the Delsarte-MacWilliams theorem compatible
subcodes of the Griesmer code, boosting the parameter capacity.
Second, we propose using a subset of the parity-check matrix of the selected
subcodes, comprising the most critical columns, to form the public matrix.
The public matrix's dimension and number of active components both increase
with the original's, but the attacker's freedom to choose from the shadows does
not. Instead, the attacker must choose from a subset of the original's columns.
Consequently, the system's security is enhanced as a result of the reduced
possible choices for the attacker. The first alteration enhances the system's
parameter capacity while maintaining its security, resulting in a significantly
more secure system.
The second alteration involves a public matrix with diminished size while
maintaining the system's original security. To demonstrate the system's
efficiency, we present three distinct instances based on specific parameter
configurations. The first is associated with the [64, 19, 3] type IV code, featuring

featuring 64 shadows and 29 information variables. The third is associated with the
[66, 33, 3] code, featuring 66 shadows and 33 information variables. The presented

study, we analyze the effects of integrating a thesaurus, which details word
meanings, into the training process of contemporary PLMs. By incorporating a
dictionary, we suggest modifying the traditional BERT training algorithm by adding
a dictionary-based objective function and representational enhancement. A new
language model, called Dict-BERT, is developed and evaluated under different
training and post-training configurations to assess its performance improvements
in several benchmark tests of semantic similarity, paraphrasing, and word sense
disambiguation experiments. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that our
proposed language model, Dict-BERT, consistently and significantly enhances
model performance in almost all the evaluation tasks and configurations. A
technically detailed description of our proposed method is provided, along

method was also tested through a pilot study where our model, Dict-BERT, was
applied to a small-scale Wikipedia dataset and yielded a substantial

validity and a range of potential applications are discussed and explored. The
results of these investigations reveal that our proposed language model, Dict-BERT,

exhibits considerable potential for real-world application. As a result, our
method may be suitable for large-scale and reliable deployment in a variety of
practical settings. The information presented in this study could be useful for
developing future theories and models of NLP. Ultimately, our investigation may

This paper highlights significant issues with Vertical Federated Learning, pointing out that it is vulnerable to several forms of privacy breach. We demonstrate two main privacy infringement methods. Firstly, a privacy breach occurring during FL protocol development can allow access to private client data, exemplified by a case where Google exposes email headers of Google Drive users as a result of participating in the formative protocol development phase. Secondly, an unauthorized agent can illicitly access or distribute aggregated federated data, illustrated by a case where Google exposes aggregated federated data of Google Drive users after gaining access through an agent. These problems not only affect users but also developers and organizations as well, with the latter two being more prominent clients of FL. We call for greater consideration of user privacy, developer, and organization privacy, and client awareness during FL implementation. Furthermore, as a potential solution, we suggest the implementation of a centralised server which unifies and secures all federated data, thereby preventing potential data leaks. This approach, validated through our analysis of Google's exposure of user data, is viewed as a gold standard for ideal vertical FL implementations. As such asynchrony is a characteristic of vertical FL, the implementation of such a centralised server or alternative solutions like Horizontal FL, could be more effective in ensuring data privacy and security. We conclude and suggest the implementation of more stringent data safety measures in vertical FL setups. 

Note: This work was recognized in the Google's Exposure of User Data section, receiving an Honorable Mention at CPM'22.

A numerical analysis of the $B$-meson decaying into a proton and a dark antibaryon was conducted using the QCD light-cone sum rules, with a key formula for the transition matrix element having been formulated first. Subsequently, the decay width was computed for $B$-mesons with various flavors as they transitioned into a proton and a dark antibaryon, with the results being compared to the standard model's decay width, specifically for the case of dark matter consisting of a proton and a dark antibaryon in the final state. It was observed that if the light-favoring scenario was assumed, the decay width would be significantly higher than what would be expected if the universality of the weak interaction was the only factor at play. Moreover, the decay width was investigated as a function of the virtuality when a dark antibaryon is formed and the results were explored using the principle of duality, with a numerical lower bound for the product of the coupling strength and dark quark mass being established. The researchers also examined the possible constraints that several theories, including leptoquark models and anarchy, could impose on the theory. Finally, the authors considered the case of "missing-momentum" in experiments at LHCb that could potentially be used to identify the channel $B\to p\bar{\Xi}^{0*}/\bar{\Omega}^0$ if the production of resonances near the threshold can be observed. If such a discovery can be made, this could open up new avenues for identifying the channel $B\to \pi\bar{\Lambda}$, with the latter being a known process involving the breaking of baryon number conservation. A future planned experiment at LHCb to study the channel $B\to J/\psi\pi$ may also be able to identify this channel, thus violating baryon number conservation at the level of tree diagrams in the standard model. The researchers conclude by discussing the challenge that dark matter, particularly that which consists of particles with masses similar to those of protons and neutrons, may pose at both theoretical and experimental levels. If future data show that matter concentrations are anisotropic on a cosmic scale, this could be used as evidence that dark matter consists of particles with masses similar to those of protons and neutrons. Researchers are therefore advised to explore the possibility of detecting such matter concentration anisotropies on a cosmic scale in the future by conducting dedicated experiments. In a Hilbert space, we devise a static Tikhonov problem with an arbitrary index m, and devise an inertial dynamics with m-regularization that incorporates damping. This combination is challenging to analyze due to the trade-off between regularization and damping. Yet, under specific conditions, we demonstrate that the solution converges strongly towards the last norm solution, even when the damping coefficient and time step are substantial. Our study involves rewriting the Tikhonov problem as a minimization task with strong duality, and leveraging the principle of majorization and minimization. This allows us to derive a lower bound on the dual objective that estimates the minimizer's proximity to the Tikhonov solution, and to convert the problem into an optimization with a non-negative outer norm. This reformulation facilitates the development of an inertial dynamics with damping that preserves its inductive properties, and to prove its strong asymptotic convergence towards the last norm solution. Moreover, under additional conditions, we verify that the solution converges at a Q-linear rate, and that the rate is better than that of mere damping. This is achieved by setting the Tikhonov problem's regularization term equal to a quadratic form involving a positive semi-definite matrix, and to convert the problem into a constrained optimization with a non-positive lower semi-definite part. This reformulation facilitates the development of an inertial dynamics with damping that preserves its inductive properties, and to prove its strong asymptotic convergence towards the last norm solution at a Q-linear rate. Numerical tests illustrate the conversion of the Tikhonov problem and the new inertial dynamics with damping, and to validate our theoretical findings. These are covered by the open-source MATLAB codes at GitHub: \url{ https://github.com/Loic-Mane/Inertial-dynamics-with-damping-to-the-Tikhonov-problem.} \end{abstract}

In modern investment, managing various asset classes is crucial to minimize risks and maximise returns through a strategy called portfolio and portfolio replication. Therefore, a method based on generative adversarial networks is proposed in this study. This method takes the mean return and volatility of a target portfolio and the number of replication portfolios as input, and generates a probability distribution of portfolio shares that meets specified conditions. These conditions include a specified level of diversity in the portfolio replication, known as complexity, and a specified level of similarity between the portfolios in different market conditions. The method uses a new type of loss function that takes into account the smoothness of the portfolio replication across different market conditions, in addition to its diversity. The effectiveness of this method is tested on a simulated dataset modelled after a stable of 9 US stock whose returns are non-symmetric and time-varying. The results show that the method not only meets the specified conditions of complexity and smoothness, but also outperforms the traditional methods in terms of the Sharpe ratio and the stability of the portfolio shares in different market conditions.
