One major drawback of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) is the high computational cost resulting from evaluating numerous candidate architectures. To mitigate this limitation, researchers often employ bias-introducing regularization methods, which set zero weights for some network components during the training process. However, using the Simple Single-Coefficient Weight (SSW) objective to select the optimal network subsstructure is not a conventional NAS technique. A thorough exploration of the SSW approach is provided in this paper, focusing on the underlying bias-induced interference patterns among network coefficients. A theoretical model is developed to analyze these interference patterns, which reveals that random noise in architecture weights can significantly impact their optimization. To overcome this constraint, the paper introduces the All-0 Gradient Regularization (A0GR) technique. A0GR adds zero gradients to some network coefficients, similar to existing methods but introduces novel selection strategies. Experimental results show that A0GR yields better performance than state-of-the-art techniques with comparable computational requirements, and is compatible with both gradient-descent and evolutionary NAS approaches. Our research explores how different novel mechanisms of electron-phonon interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. We propose a new concept called Fermi surface harmonic coupling, where a significant number of phonons have a major impact on valley switching time due to a valley-dependent anharmonic effect, which is more pronounced at room temperature. We found that another novel interaction, gecko coupling, also affects valley persistence using a new form of coupling that goes beyond conventional point-like interactions. We established a key relationship between phonon frequency and electron-phonon coupling constant and showed that gecko coupling contributes significantly to valley preservation. We discovered that gecko coupling arises from two new novel interaction mechanisms, umklapp scattering related harmonic coupling and short-range interaction-induced gecko coupling. We found that umklapp scattering related harmonic coupling contributes a significant amount at low temperatures and short-range interaction-induced gecko coupling contributes a significant amount at high temperatures. We showed that another novel interaction, related to plasmon-phonon coupling, also affects valley persistence. We discovered that this interaction contributes a significant amount at high temperatures. We used these results to estimate an upper limit for the performance of valley-based electronics. Our research demonstrates the importance of non-conventional mechanisms of electron-phonon interaction in two-dimensional materials and their potential to re-evaluate the performance of valley-based electronics. Using a public database and an open-source coding as suggested in ref. 32, our code is provided for the umklapp scattering related harmonic coupling and gecko coupling interactions. However, the research on the short-range interaction-induced gecko coupling and plasmon-phonon coupling is originally presented in this work. As these novel interaction mechanisms are an extension of conventional interactions, our calculations rely solely on the conventional parameters of phonon coupling. However, the research indicates that the conventional understanding of electron-phonon coupling is insufficient to fully account for the behavior of valley physics in two-dimensional materials. We have conducted extensive diagrammatic Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the Fermi polaron model in two-dimensional space. Our calculations prioritize paired diagrams and rigorously apply the conserving equations from many-body theory. The outcomes demonstrate that at zero temperature, our approach successfully predicts a continuous critical point between the polaron and deformed Fermi liquid phases, consistent with quantum field theory predictions. Moreover, our study shows the effects of temperature and interaction strength on the polaron's properties and reveals the evolution of the critical point with temperature. Comparisons with existing theoretical and experimental results confirm the veracity of our approach. The ability of the diagrammatic Monte Carlo method to capture diverse many-body phenomena makes it a versatile tool for exploring various phases and critical points within complex Fermi systems. It can be applied to a wide range of scenarios, such as pairing and magnetic phase transitions, as well as to intricate quantum states like superconductivity, magnetism, and topological order. Future applications of this method involve uncovering underlying phase diagrams in a variety of systems, as described in the last section. In the hybrid digital-analog computing technique, an analog quantum register is utilized along with a digital component, offering adaptability in implementing quantum algorithms. This method is particularly beneficial when dealing with systems of interconnected particles, as seen in the quantum simulation of a complex fermionic system. Through analog quantum processing, the physical connections among particles are directly accounted for, as opposed to the digital method which requires explicit computation of interactions. A proposed hybrid fermionic simulation scheme leverages analog qubits and quantum connections to represent fermionic operators, ultimately relying on measurement to derive fermionic expectation values. Recently, a digital scheme for fermionic simulation was developed to compete effectively with analog implementations. However, this study shows that the digital scheme can be simplified into a more efficient model and that the hybrid digital-analog approach offers improved results. Specifically, our method reduces T gate number by approximately $40\%$, decreases the number of T^2 gates by $25\%$, and decreases the number of ancillary qubits by $20\%$ in comparison to the digital scheme inspired by IP-QA. This improvement in performance lays the foundation for executing more complex quantum simulations and further algorithmic developments in the future. A future roadmap for implementation on NISQ devices is also outlined, including suggestions for both NISQ-aware research and hardware requirements. A key take-home point is that the hybrid approach may provide better outcomes compared to standalone digital or analog quantum simulations of fermionic systems. Furthermore, our method for fermionic simulation does not rely on any specific physical implementation and can be applied across various quantum computing architectures. Our primary goal in this research is to develop a new set of points on the surface of a unit sphere by using points from existing distributions. We propose the'stitching technique', which allows us to generate these new sets of points. Furthermore, we utilize various point distributions to create spherical domains with different geometric properties. We then apply the stitching technique to the surfaces of spherical domains to create sets of points. Notably, our method can preserve the local density of points in the original distribution. We introduce several examples of spherical domains with unique characteristics, such as those with hollow centers, multiple regions divided by deep depressions, and regions with gradually changing thickness. We also create sets of points on these domains using the stitching technique. In addition to the stitching technique, we develop another method to create spherical domains by expanding clusters of points from uniform distributions on the surface of a unit sphere. We evaluate the effectiveness of these methods through visualizations and statistical analysis. We demonstrate that our approaches outperform existing techniques in generating suitable data for neural network training in supervised contexts. We utilize point distributions generated via kernel-based replication from two types of original distributions: uniform and bivariate normal. We create fields from these point distributions and utilize sorting algorithms to create point sets on the surface of a unit sphere with distinct density gradients. We evaluate the quality of the generated data for neural network training by comparing it with the quality of data generated by drawing random points from a uniform distribution as a reference. Notably, our method significantly outperforms the reference in terms of performance. We start with point sets from uniform and bivariate normal distributions as Bresler-Larson points and Bresler-Larson clusters, respectively. We apply a Poisson integrator to generate field values on fine lattices from these point sets. A comprehensive understanding of quantum dynamics within complex many-body systems is crucial but remains elusive due to the computational intractability problem. A suitable approach to tackle this challenge is to analyze the scaling of the propagator in the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, which we can achieve by utilizing a statistical mechanical framework by introducing a fractality-sensitive term coupled with the system's Hamiltonian. Our proposal is centered around the Kondo model because it allows us to study the effects of two critical shifts, related to Kondo and many-body localization temperatures, in a controllable manner. Furthermore, the proposed method can be applied to other models and phenomena. The problem of computing real-time correlation functions is a major obstacle in this context, and we suggest a new strategy based on the scaling of the propagator to overcome this issue, thus enabling the construction of dynamical density-correlation functions even in deep the ergodicity gap of the many-body localization phase. As a proof of concept, we propose a semi-classical approximation that helps to gain insight into scaling functions and fractality parameters. By extrapolating this approximation, we can estimate parameters such as the critical exponent lambda, which describes the scaling of correlation lengths, and the multifractal exponent alpha_0 defined through the scaling function alpha(D)/log N. As the transition to renewable energy and flexible resources (such as energy storage) gains momentum, the electric power sector is undergoing a significant shift globally.  However, current power system models used to analyze this transition often fail to consider key aspects of their output, including subnational detail and specific technology mix.  In this paper, we investigate how these models respond to varying scenarios of resource deployment and discover that nearly all models can accommodate high shares of renewable energy - over 1000 GW in the US and over 800 GW in Germany.  Additionally, our research reveals that certain models can provide detailed information on specific technology mixes, such as solar and storage within regions, while others can simulate local detail down to the state or even municipal level.  Furthermore, our analysis shows a strong link between model responsiveness and the strength of local policy support for clean energy production.  We also identify specific characteristics of resource mix that influence a model's performance and provide policy recommendations for enhancing the output of power system models used to inform energy and policy decisions.  This study offers critical insights for users of these models, including industry stakeholders, researchers, and policymakers, potentially enabling them to gather more accurate and detailed information to support their work.  It also opens the door for further research into the limitations of power system models and how to overcome them.  In particular, our work suggests that developing new models is a promising area of investigation.  Ultimately, through our careful evaluation of power system models, we aim to promote greater transparency and understanding in the field.  This study and its findings are intended to serve as a valuable resource and starting point for users of these models and for those looking to develop more effective and accurate model scenarios.  Moreover, our research provides essential insights for users of power system models to tailor their analysis and interpretation of model outcomes to specific policy goals and requirements.  This study is part of a larger project, the Comparative Assessment of Power system Expansion Models and Impacts.  This project seeks to advance knowledge and provide important contributions to the field of power system modeling and analysis. Software developers widely use search techniques initially to understand unfamiliar code, 
and researchers have studied these practices through extensive empirical research. 
A key aspect of search is deciding specific, relevant keywords to input into the code 
search interface, a process known as the 'keyword selection task.' 
Although prior studies have examined under-defined or over-defined search scenarios, 
a lack of research exists on the third search scenario, where relevant information 
is available, yet researchers remain uncertain about exactly what specific aspects 
constitute relevant information. 
In such situations, developers might carry out information retrieval-based concept 
location, a technique that is not entirely new. 
This present study is known as STRICT, a heuristic method for identifying relevant 
search keywords through a structured analysis of IR-based concept location. 
The proposed approach was tested on 1,051 Java methods from 16 scientific papers. 
As a result, a significant 77.4% improvement was seen in the quality of selected 
search keywords in comparison to an existing null hypothesis method. 
The proposed approach was found to be efficient, taking an average of less than 2 
minutes per method to complete. 
Post-study interviews with 11 software professionals revealed that a key enabler for 
using such an IR-based approach was not cost, but rather the ability to integrate 
external tools. 
Multiple potential applications for STRICT were also discovered, including refining 
existing search methods and providing new hypotheses for under-defined search 
scenarios. 
The study's findings open up further areas for improvement, in particular further 
empirical studies to confirm the results, as well as exploring other tool integrations 
that could broaden the user base for such techniques. 
Ultimately, the study suggests that such approaches could be accessible to developers 
if adequately streamlined.

The Collatz Conjecture is a mathematical hypothesis concerning a sequence of numbers, also known as the 3x+1 problem. This hypothesis states that any sequence of integers starting from a given number and applying a series of rules can only reach zero. The rules involve either tripling the number and adding one or simply taking one, and the conjecture suggests that no matter what initial value is chosen, the rules will always result in a sequence that ends at zero. There are programs and documents that have tested and explored these sequences up to extremely large numbers, and the conjecture remains that there should be no counterexamples, however a rigorous mathematical proof has yet to be found. The potential behind this type of number has led to a variety of studies spanning physics, biology, and even the potential for complex systems to organize themselves in a self-similar manner. The article will look at some of the most recent developments and proposals for a proof or further research ideas related to this type of number. The goal is not to present the most advanced ideas but rather a general overview while avoiding more mature or recent ideas to allow for younger mathematicians to explore this type of number. The central issue in the stable matching concept is to identify the optimal match between individuals or entities with distinct preferences, yet in reality, we only have a limited number of potential matches in mind. This limited perspective prompts the question: Should we maintain the option to consider more suits in the future, even if there's no direct match at present? This idea is denoted by the term "free choice." Conversely, the concept of "irreversible commitment" suggests that, once a decision is made, further considerations are ruled out. This research investigates the trade-offs between various stable matching algorithms under both the conditions of having multiple suits to consider and the constraint of making no future matches. An analysis of the algorithms under the "free choice" condition reveals that, in order to guarantee stability, the number of possible matches in the current instance must be at least equal to the size of the largest possible matching cluster. This requirement is shown to be necessary and not the outcome of any specific preference profile. An examination of the "irreversible commitment" condition uncovers instances where size-$n$ preferences still result in unstable matches, even for the largest possible matching cluster. Moreover, prior research that utilized pre-processing to find a match in a size-$n$ subset of the preferences is also found to be suboptimal. This research demonstrates that pre-processing to consider all preferences in order has better performance guarantees than this pre-processing-based approach. Finally, an investigation of intercardinal-weight stable matching in size-$n$ preferences under the "irreversible commitment" condition uncovers that, in some cases, a size-$n$ preference profile leads to the scenario where every individual with a large rank has a match while those with a lower rank do not. This situation is denoted by the term "bad-intercardinal-weight" preference profile. A detailed analysis of the characteristics of such profiles reveals that they are quite common, with approximately $\frac{1}{n}$ of all size-$n$ profiles featuring this property for large $n$. Moreover, "bad-intercardinal-weight" profiles are shown to be quite prevalent among size-$n$ preferences even when a size-$n$ rank-optimal match exists. An analysis of the algorithms under the "irreversible commitment" condition reveals that established post-processing-based approaches to cardinal-weight stable matching algorithms are found to be suboptimal in certain situations. In fact, some of these algorithms sacrifice too much in terms of overall happiness for the sake of fairness. Consequently, a simpler algorithm is proposed and evaluated

The origin of the dissipation range in the energy spectrum of geophysical fluids like the ocean and atmosphere has been linked to the production of infinite vortices, a concept introduced by the author in 2018 as a theoretical framework. This framework is based on the infinite vortices hypothesis, which suggests that fluid turbulence arises from the disturbance of thermal currents moving upward in the atmosphere's troposphere. The model proposes that the motion of molecules near the thermal equilibrium state creates an invisible, infinite vortical field, which is not part of the fluid's velocity field. The interaction between this energy and the turbulence's kinetic energy is believed to be the cause of the dissipation range in the energy spectrum. The existence of infinite vortices explains various turbulent phenomena that have remained unresolvable for decades, particularly in the atmospheric science community. This study revisits the theoretical model that supports the statistical model of the atmospheric energy spectrum as proposed by the author in 2018. The model was further developed in a paper published in 2020, which provided a theoretical basis for the -5/3 slope in the atmospheric surface spectrum within the dissipation range. The proposed TDIV hypothesis is designed to integrate the three scales of atmospheric observation, resulting in a to-scale model of the atmospheric energy spectrum that combines three distinct breaking wave patterns into a single expression. The to-scale model is shown to provide an accurate fit to the entire atlas of atmospheric surface spectra compiled by the University of Colorado's Professor McCaughey. Professor Kerry Emanuel, a renowned expert in atmospheric modeling, provided a mathematical representation of the vorticity production term due to infinite vortices, which forms the basis of the to-scale model in this study. The model reveals that the atmospheric surface spectrum is composed of three distinct breaking wave patterns, which together create the energy shift observed near 10-meter altitude in Professor McCaughey's atlas. This shift is attributed to a critical velocity of approximately 0.25 meters per second, which marks the boundary between two distinct breaking wave patterns. The higher wave pattern above this boundary is responsible for the energy observed in the atmosphere's surface spectrum within the dissipation range below 0.1 meters. The model also identifies a critical strain of approximately 0.01 as a second determining factor of the energy spectrum's behavior within the dissipation range, which results from the interaction between infinite vortices and the turbulence's kinetic energy, resulting in an additional higher wave pattern. The interaction between an ultrashort laser pulse and a transparent liquid results in the formation of a localized temperature gradient, which may lead to the appearance of self-induced diffraction patterns. This diffraction result from optical nonlinearity is identifiable as either a sharp peak or a zeroth-order dip, which can be predicted based on the refractive index change along the laser beam path. This change is caused by the laser-induced temperature profile, which follows the heat equation in the liquid. By solving this equation with simultaneous laser pulse absorption and thermal conductivity, the temperature gradient becomes a function of two variables: time and spatial location. This study numerically models these variables to assess their impact on the laser self-induced diffraction pattern, which may involve nonlinear interactions between laser waves. This analysis involves refractive index relationships and their role in laser self-induced diffraction patterns. This research provides a foundation for understanding laser self-induced diffraction in liquids and their applications. The problem of recovering missing features in streaming tenor loops is crucial for real-time visual data restoration, a task that we investigate in this paper. We address this challenge by developing a novel algorithm called Patch Tracking-based Streaming Tensor Loop Completion (PST-LoCo). Distinguishing it from prior studies that assume complete and balanced data entry, our proposed method is designed for incomplete and unbalanced data entry, eliminating the need for data buffering. PST-LoCo leverages superdiagonal Frobenius norm minimization, combining patch-based feature tracking and low-rank tensor completion techniques to ensure accurate and efficient recovery of missing features. Thoroughly evaluated using real-world datasets and contrasting it with state-of-the-art methods that require data buffering, our proposed approach achieves superior performance in both efficiency and accuracy. Moreover, we have successfully applied PST-LoCo to unbalanced data entry, expanding its practical usability. Additionally, our method utilizes a novel patch-based feature tracking technique that surpasses current state-of-the-art methods for determining patch size. The source code for this study is publicly available at https://github.com/baile-yu/PST-LoCo. Experiment results demonstrate that PST-LoCo achieves an mAE of 0.4486 and mPE of 0.1129 on the SMT dataset and an mAE of 0.6541 and mPE of 0.1835 on the SDDataset. Furthermore, our results indicate that PST-LoCo processes 200 frames per second on the SMT dataset and 40 frames per second on the SDDataset. Recent years have witnessed the proliferation of studies on image understanding with machines. Conversely, there's a notable absence of research examining the role of severe image transformations from the human perspective. This oversight limits our understanding of the distinctive capabilities and shortcomings of human and machine visual systems. In this study, a unique set of 19 extreme transformations is introduced, aimed at creating novel and complex images while retaining essential visual elements. These results are then compared across three distinct frameworks: human perception, human-created categories, and machine-driven approaches. Our research highlights the differing responses to these extreme transformations from the perspectives of human vision and artificial visual systems, providing valuable insights for future research in image transform techniques. We have developed the 'High-z Sudoku' method, a tool for verifying the accuracy of redshift measurements in spectral line scans within the millimeter wavelength range. By leveraging the distinct patterns of thermal broadening, we generate hypothetical redshift distributions in front of spectral lines and assess whether observed data, such as those from ALMA, JCMT, and NOEMA, align with these scenarios. Our approach is particularly suitable for unresolved sources, where line broadening can be accurately described. As a test, we applied the High-z Sudoku method to three benchmark datasets and found one spurious redshift among eight measurements. Our algorithm is available on GitHub under the name 'high_z_sudoku'. We believe that High-z Sudoku, in conjunction with machine learning and human judgment, can form a powerful three-component system for identifying and verifying redshifts. Our study has specific recommendations for improving the accuracy of redshift measurements in future studies. Furthermore, we have used the High-z Sudoku method to identify optimal observational settings for upcoming experiments, such as RECIPE. By implementing these settings, we can increase the likelihood of at least 90% of all redshift measurements being correct. Recent breakthroughs in natural language processing have led to significant improvements in translating phrases into logical forms. Nevertheless, the existing approaches are hindered by their reliance on substantial datasets and proprietary tools for logic, making them incompatible with current NLP nomenclature and limiting their applicability to real-world applications. Our work aims to create semantic interpreters that are aligned with the latest NLP frameworks and can operate freely without relying on logic. We have developed a new, non-logic based semantic parser that is trained directly from text, and our tests reveal its capabilities even when working with very limited data. Additionally, our interpreter is capable of producing output in diverse formats, ranging from tree structures to more modular forms. Furthermore, our research demonstrates its ability to function effectively in two complex environments: a system designed to translate phrases into logical forms and a system intended to analyze sentence meanings. Our final experiment involves putting the interpreter to use in a machine that translates phrases into logical forms. Importantly, our research discovers that the interpreter's performance can be enhanced by leveraging its ability to explain phrases in ways that are easy to understand. This new approach is set to revolutionize the field by enabling the creation of semantic interpreters even in situations where the explanations provided are imperfect or incomplete. We analyzed the newly acquired X-ray data spanning from 2020 to 2021 and compared them to historical observations, revealing significant variability.  High-circularized-excess counts, variable hardness, and changing spectral shapes have emerged, further distinguishing this active low-mass black hole from its high-mass counterpart.  Three distinct energy states have been observed: a high-active state characterized by high X-ray counts along with significant soft and hard X-ray emission; a lower-active state visible in earlier years with lower X-ray counts and softer spectra; and an off-state exhibited in Chandra data with the lowest X-ray counts and the softest spectra.  We investigated multiple scenarios for the activation of the off-state state, including an ejecta/ripening scenario vs. a flaring activity scenario, and observed that the activation of the off-state state occurs more frequently during the flaring activity scenario. A 3D photonic band gap reflector effectively enhanced absorption in the thicker silicon film (approximately 510 nm) by redirecting wasted transmission into the substrate into the sample. In this setting, the highest absorption achieved was 98%, and this was stable across a wide range of incident angles. Furthermore, the same back reflector effectively increased photoconductive absorption in the thinner silicon film (approximately 260 nm) by converting reflected light from the substrate into the sample into absorbed radiation within the film. In this case, the highest absorption observed was 85%, and this was dependent on the incident angle, peaking at a 10-degree angle. Our study reveals that a back reflector is crucial for thin and ultrathin silicon films and enables efficient photothermal and photoconductive absorption through simple and affordable methods. In recommender systems, users' interactions with items are typically modeled using collaborative filtering methods that capture shared preferences among users and items. However, these methods have limitations, as they don't consider the reasons behind users' sequence of actions. Therefore, it's beneficial to develop systems that can learn users' underlying motivations, or purposes, particularly in sequential recommendation settings. Here, we present an novel approach called Latent User Purpose Modeling, or LUPM, which uses a user-item sequence representation to determine both the recommended items and the hidden causes behind users' behavior. By introducing a goal-aware space where user-items reside and purposes are defined, LUPM uses an adaptive goal assignment mechanism to assign each user-item pair to a specific goal in sequence. This approach is accomplished through a shared goal assignment layer that dynamically sets goals for every user-item transition and a goal assignment regression layer that retroactively assigns goals for evaluation. LUPM achieves improved performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on two real-world datasets and is visually illustrated through an experimental study that demonstrates both qualitatively and quantitatively how it captures users' underlying motivations, or purposes. When users' motivations are understood, the system is able to make more accurate recommendations. By examining DOO as a social club with member benefits, our research examines incentives for users to join and stay on such platforms. From a theoretical perspective, we compare the total value of benefits that members receive on DOO with the costs associated, including the risk of liquidation and potential platform downtime. Empirical evidence from five DOOs confirms that users are motivated to use these platforms by the expected benefits, which highlights the importance of ensuring platform security to maintain user trust. Additionally, our findings suggest that users are particularly sensitive to large liquidation losses and that small advantages in security can have a substantial impact on user adoption. Furthermore, we have discovered an interesting phenomenon, known as "chicken-and-egg," which may hinder the growth of DOOs, which can only function effectively when they have both sufficient liquidity and security, which can be challenging to achieve in practice. Overall, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the benefits and costs associated with using DOOs and offers insights that can be used to guide the design and management of decentralized trading platforms. The results presented can be applied not only to DOOs but also to other decentralized trading platforms, including Generalized Order Book Markets (GOMs), which represent a potential next step in the evolution of DOOs. A novel framework has been introduced for analyzing data with missing values using a Bayesian approach. The E-value metric, based on Kullback-Leibler divergence, measures similarity between distributions, was used to compare observed and predicted distributions. Predictions were generated using two imputation techniques, mean imputation and Bayesian estimation. The Bayesian estimation approach assumes multivariate normal data and estimates means and covariance matrices. Our analysis involved (1) a purely Bayesian method that compares observed and predicted E-values to determine relevance; (2) a method that combines frequentist and Bayesian assessments of relevance, identified through a significance test, and weighted by p-values. The effectiveness of these methods was demonstrated through simulations and a real-world study focusing on colorectal cancer risk factors. The source code is publicly available on our GitHub repository. The methods identified relevant age and gender variables at optimal thresholds, similar to frequentist methods. The Bayesian approach was found to be more robust to variable missing data, while the blended method retained sensitivity control. The Bayesian estimation technique produced narrower confidence intervals than traditional maximum likelihood estimators, although the differences were minor. Ultimately, the Bayesian approach emerged as a reliable solution for missing data analysis, offering a balance of interpretability, flexibility, and accuracy. The findings were discussed in the context of ethical research practices. The rising demand for tiny cryogenic systems capable of maintaining millikelvin temperatures is driven by the growing influence of quantum information research, particularly in the areas of quantum computing and quantum communication. This research discusses the development of a large cryogenic system, dubbed 'Cryotrain,' designed to facilitate experimental work at superconducting magnet facilities like the Fermilab Quantum Computing Testbed for superconducting devices that operate at very low temperatures. Achieving a high level of vibration damping was crucial for creating a stable cryogenic environment, which could be accomplished by introducing the Cryotrain into a cryogenic transfer container filled with superfluid helium. This research outlines techniques for enhancing the stability of cryogenic environments and demonstrates a successful demonstration of the Cryotrain at an acceleration rate of 0.1 K/h using a combination of its 10 components, each with distinct functionality. A comparison of predicted and actual temperature distributions within the system helped validate numerical models used to design the Cryotrain's cryogenic environment. This research discusses various applications for the Cryotrain, including extensions of the cryogenic environment to support multiple superconducting devices in parallel and extensions to integrate new cryogenic components capable of storing multiple amounts of liquid helium. This architecture for integrating quantum devices, termed 'cryotrain modules,' lays the foundation for a scalable and compact cryogenic system to be used at the Quantum Computing Testbed. This approach for extending cryogenic systems and numerical modeling of its components can be applied more broadly to the development of cryogenic systems for quantum computing applications. Additionally, the effectiveness of useful techniques for managing cryogenic systems that operate at low temperatures and maintain cryogenic stability are discussed. A future plan to use the Cryotrain at the Quantum Computing Testbed involves testing it with cryogenic devices that are capable of maintaining millikelvin temperatures, potentially including devices developed by Quantum Technologies, LLC and IBM. This testing will involve using the Cryotrain to rapidly change superconducting device frequencies in response to changes in the magnetic environment, similar to a quantum spin switch, a component that is becoming increasingly in demand at the Quantum Computing Testbed. This research and testing at rapidly changing magnetic environments and the effects on superconducting devices that rely on magnetic fields for operation, particularly SQUIDs and transmon qubits. An accompanying movie shows the Cryotrain being used at Fermilab and demonstrates its capacity to maintain its stability in a high-speed environment. This research highlights the significance of accurately modeling cryogenic environments and achieving a high level of stability within these environments

Previous research highlights the prevalence of mistakes in cryptographic software libraries, indicating they are found in a significant proportion of programs that use cryptography. In contrast, fault introduction techniques, which are designed by attackers to exploit weaknesses in programs, are relatively rare. This study conducts the first comprehensive assessment of malicious code that exploits cryptographic vulnerabilities: It analyzes 1,553 unique Python functions from 847 malware samples, including 604 cryptographers' functions from Python Crypto and Cryptography Hacker's Handbook, and 949 function calls from 847 unique malware samples. The analysis shows that malware authors use cryptographic functions without knowledge of the underlying algorithm in 41% of cases, demonstrate a lack of understanding of common cryptographic algorithms in 33% of cases, apply incorrect preprocessing to input in 31% of cases, fail to remove sensitive data after processing in 30% of cases, and expose sensitive data in 24% of cases. The research further examines the algorithms used by Python Crypto and Python Crypto C APIs, identifying common weaknesses, such as poor support for hash functions other than SHA-256 and SHA-256 in 41% of cases, weak key generation in 33% of cases through the use of default salt values, insufficient entropy in 33% of cases, failure to validate input in 31% of cases, and exposure of sensitive data in 24% of cases. The authors note that real-world attackers rarely misuse cryptographic algorithms, likely because introducing misuses is more difficult than exploiting vulnerabilities. They suggest that best practices for secure cryptography should be widely adopted by malware authors, indicating the algorithms currently considered secure can be considered unbreakable. In addition, the analysis provides practitioners with a guide to evaluating the security of existing and custom cryptographic implementations, providing a secure alternative to the insecure algorithms currently supported. The analysis was conducted as part of BibTeX@CC project to assess the security of various programming languages' cryptographic implementations. A novel evaluation method is introduced that does not rely on source code control as does the existing assessment methods. Instead, the authors retrieve and analyze malware samples through automated testing, allowing them to assess implementations not shared with the community, or those that use third party libraries. However, extracting actionable information from these floods of data requires sophisticated data analysis tools to aid city planners in making informed decisions. In seismic reflectivity inversion, the objective of \ell1\,norm-based sparse seismic inversion is to suppress details below a specified resolution, but the lack of a clear strategy for determining the optimal sparsity level makes it difficult to set an appropriate threshold. This paper proposes a novel deep learning-based two-step method, referred to as the NuSPAN process, to address this problem. The method initially applies SPAdes, a state-of-the-art model to generate contiguously spanning subsets of data, to enhance sparse proxy approximations. A learned convolutional neural network then employs a learned \ell1\,norm-based optimization scheme to derive the optimal sparsity proxy for the original sparse objective. The method's utility in seismic inversion is further validated by its capacity to achieve superior outcomes in comparison to conventional optimization methods and other supervised learning techniques. Additionally, the research highlights the applicability of the SPAdes tool in other areas of significant interest, such as super-resolution image enhancement and multi-channel removal of interference. Automated part-of-speech (POS) tagging is a widely used task in linguistics, often applied to modern language. The advent of machine learning has significantly enhanced POS tagging, but its current models are heavily influenced by large amounts of recent data. This is problematic, as most existing annotation methods are no longer applicable to older texts using today's models. To overcome this challenge, we developed new machine learning methods that can accurately apply modern POS categories to historical text, despite the significant differences in language. Our methods recognize that certain POS categories are rarely or never used in historical text, and instead, we allow for a range of possible replacements. The success of these models was tested on two corpora from 16th and 19th century French literature. The top-performing method achieved an average accuracy of 44.8% and a median accuracy of 41.9%. Additionally, we found that our proposed system was more reliable than existing automatic annotation methods, while also being highly adaptable to different time periods through set-based annotation. As a result, we were able to successfully apply our methods to various subsets of two extensive collections of 16th century French text. A novel quantum error correction approach, the hidden inverses protocol, is introduced and demonstrated on real superconducting quantum devices using the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state and entangling gates. The hidden inverses protocol operates without necessitating error correction gates, instead using a quantum register initially in a computational basis state and incorporating gates that incorporate the inverse of affected gates to correct errors. The protocol is tested on a two-qubit device initially in a computational basis state with insertion of an X gate and subsequent SWAP and Z rotation gates, where the counter-gates CXad and Zad are found to correct the errors, revealing the application's viability for quantum error correction. The hidden inverses protocol is particularly useful in quantum computing systems lacking an error correction unit due to the absence of required error correction gates, reducing implementation costs. The protocol is tested on a multi-qubit protocol involving the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state with insertion of highly interdependent CXad gates and show the protocol's applicability and efficiency in complex quantum systems. The protocol is particularly useful in quantum computing systems lacking an error correction unit due to the absence of required error correction gates, thus reducing implementation costs. The protocol's feasibility highlights its capacity to correct intricate quantum errors independently of how the errors arose, thus making it a valuable tool for correcting quantum errors across a wide array of quantum computing systems without modification. The protocol's efficiency in correcting errors on complex quantum systems was found to be high, thus making it a viable option for near-term devices. The protocol's applicability to near-term devices is particularly appealing as it does not demand the deployment of error-active gates. However, existing toolsets for this field are often incompatible, platform-specific, 
and lacking standardization which causes significant issues for developers, 
comprises major bottlenecks for wider usage, and hinders model outputs that can be 
utilized by healthcare professionals for precise clinical decision-making.

these challenges through its support for standard encoding of digital images and model 
outputs in pathology and radiomics, utilizing standard DICOM and CHAOS terminology. 
This library provides users with easy access to current model outputs, simplifies 
model adoption, enhances model understanding and transparency, and provides an 
efficient channel for model deployment. 
Highdicom includes a pathologic model output example based on the classification 
of colorectal cisplatin-resistant lymph node metastases through a novel analytical 
approach that combines quantitative circadian variability and cytokine analysis, 
as well as a radiomics example related to liver lesions, which highlights the 
library's functionality.

The exponential growth of genomic data demands efficient methods for extracting features from DNA sequences. A significant number of existing DNA analysis tasks, including protein function prediction and gene classification, can be performed effectively using specialized neural networks that process raw genomic data. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of these networks depends on the quality of representations extracted during the pre-training phase, a critical step in making genomic data usable with off-the-shelf deep learning models. To address this challenge, we introduce an unsupervised feature learning method for DNA sequences based on the DeepSeq approach originally designed for text data. Our enhanced technique, DeepSeqGen, incorporates a Contextual Self-Attention mechanism, a Kernels-for-Position model, and a Positional Dropout handler, all of which enable our model to capture global and local patterns in DNA sequences and generate contextual, position-aware representations. We evaluate the accuracy of DeepSeqGen by applying it to downstream tasks, including binary classification and regression, and compare its performance to other established unsupervised feature learning methods for DNA sequences. The results demonstrate that DeepSeqGen achieves superior results, outperforming other methods in multiple downstream tasks. Notably, when applied to a critical downstream task, DeepSeqGen accurately identifies misannotated cas13a genes with an AUC-PR of 0.82, a significant improvement over the previously reported AUC-PR of 0.41. The DeepSeqGen model, along with accompanying computational tools and data, is publicly available at the following repository: https://github.com/ashariz/DeepSeqGen. The computational analysis described in this research is documented and made accessible at the following ZENODO repository: https://doi.org/10.35415/2022msc012. (UMGC-2022-00012). This gives rise to two distinct types of symmetric Dyck trails, which are used to construct examples of symmetric Dyck paths with unique ordinary partition limits. By extending the q-analog of the partition function, we establish a result regarding the number of Dyck trails in a particular region of the Dyck ladder, and this result has a significant implication for the chromatic symmetric functions. Finally, we show that the Dyck--Chapman region associated with a Dyck path can be represented as a sum of the chromatic symmetric functions of two Dyck trails whose endpoints differ by a reflection. This relationship provides a basis for computing the ordinary limits of symmetric Dyck trails with a specific symmetry property. Moreover, the structure of the Dyck--Chapman region associated with a reflection pair is connected to the number of ways in which a row contains all the elements of a colored partition. We've noticed that standard convolutional networks often fail to differentiate between images that are rotated from one another. In response, we've developed the Direction Convolutional Network, which incorporates directional convolution components that expand an image's representation into multiple directions. This design allows the network to recognize rotated images by treating different rotation directions as distinct features. Our DIRENet architecture consists of modules that perform convolution along circular trajectories in the spatial domain and also aligns the principal direction of each layer's representation across all channels. Our experiments indicate that our method can achieve competitive results on rotation recognition tasks on CIFAR-10 and DTD datasets. Moreover, we've found that the intermediate representations produced by DIRENet in the MOCO 1:1 pre-training scenario contain information about image direction. Therefore, the direction knowledge can be utilized as an unsupervised image representation that bridges the domain gap in unsupervised domain adaptation problems. Our proposed method, the Redirection challenge, outperforms state-of-the-art methods and significantly improves unsupervised domain adaptation performance on various datasets. First, by establishing Regge-type relationships for the light meson distribution amplitudes, and second, by extracting the S-wave factorization coefficients of three-body momenta in light mesons using non-relativistic QCD and perturbative QCD, thereby quantifying the role of the light quark masses. Determining the top quark-pole mass using perturbative QCD constraints based on deep inelastic scattering data, and taking into account the effects of the light quarks on the gluon PDF and the perturbative evolution of the top quark PDF, we found that variations in the light quark mass and PDFs result in alterations to the top quark mass of no more than 0.5 GeV, a crucial consideration for precise top quark mass measurements in support of the Higgs boson studies. Furthermore, our study highlights the significance of incorporating corrections due to the light quarks when extracting top quark mass from various top quark-related observables such as $m_t$ from dijet events or single top quark production. Currently, the primary tools for identifying COVID-19 in chest computed tomography (CT) scans rely on manual or automated diagnostic methods that lack consistency and often require prolonged processing times. Recent research has shown that machine learning models can effectively detect COVID-19, but they require large amounts of data and still exhibit room for improvement. To develop a human-equivalent COVID-19 detection method from low-dose CT scans, we proposed a two-stage time-distributed capsule network model. By leveraging the capabilities of capsule networks, which combine the advantages of convolutional and recurrent neural networks, we designed a model that could learn and predict the temporal relationships within multi-slice scans efficiently. Experimental results demonstrated that our model consistently produced diagnoses, could be applied to individual slices or the entire scan, and had the potential to enhance detection capabilities when augmented with magnetic resonance imaging data. Furthermore, our model's performance parameters indicated that it was equivalent to or superior to the current best-performing models, with an ROC-AUC score of 0.9686 and the loss reduced by 9.9% by using our approach to train the model incrementally. A novel dataset has been developed that maps the location of satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) by transponders, providing continuous updates on their spatial positioning. Using this data, a graph can be constructed where nodes represent spherical sections of space and edges represent movements between these areas. Subsequently, a method for identifying vacant areas in the graph was developed, which can be utilized to either prevent or detect unauthorized access to these spots, or take advantage of them as available resources. It has been observed that the density of satellite movements in the graph is concentrated in areas closer to Earth, indicating a significant reduction in the required transponder count for space monitoring with the introduction of just a single operational spacecraft. Our study focuses on identifying the optimal spherical sections to be monitored by each transponder and makes use of a greedy algorithm for this purpose. It is found that on average, each transponder requires monitoring at most 257 out of 4096 spherical sections, and that the transponder coverage area can overlap with other transponders' coverage in 50% of the areas, potentially enabling the realization of a global monitoring system. It is also found that the space monitoring capability can be achieved with a significantly reduced number of transponders, namely 17, which is far lower than the 68 required for passive monitoring. Furthermore, when engaging in active monitoring, a single spacecraft can be utilized to provide coverage without the need for any transponders. This study also explores the potential for using this space monitoring framework in other orbital zones and for reentering objects, and it highlights the significance of taking into account the varying number of spherical sections in different zones when designing the monitoring graph. A potential extension of this work involves incorporating the impact of space object motion simplifications on the graph construction for non-keplerian objects. The study also sheds light on the relationship between space monitoring and the conflict-resolution problem in the cap set, showing that the density of movements in the graph in areas closer to Earth is similar to the access structure density in the case of no motion simplification. Moreover, it is found that the space monitoring graph density is comparable to the conflict graph density in areas far from Earth. In addition, it is shown that the optimal conflict-resolution strategy for reentry objects involves assigning the entire area to the last observed transponder, and that the space monitoring framework can be applied to resolve conflicts for reentry objects starting from various initial positions by incorporating the force applied to the space object. To address these complexities, a comprehensive strategy is proposed for generating refined meshes on CAD models. This method combines the constraints inherent in the design domain with the constraints imposed by entities in the product geometry. Additionally, the strategy optimizes mesh node placements within the domain to minimize the resulting mesh, taking into consideration both the constraint-related costs and the spatial arrangement of mesh nodes. To achieve this, a mixed-integer linear programming model is developed, which allows for the optimal placement of mesh nodes under various constraints. At the outset of the mesh generation process, a initial coarse mesh is obtained through this optimization-based approach. Subsequently, a refined detailed mesh is generated by adaptively refining the initial coarse mesh using local refinements and local re-meshing operations. To facilitate the mesh refinement process, the strategy relies on a novel approach for determining the optimal locations and shapes of mesh triangles within the design domain in order to optimize the resulting mesh. The strategy also incorporates a robust mechanism for dynamically updating the mesh triangle orientations in response to constraints arising from the product geometry as the mesh generation process progresses. Consequently, the resulting meshes obtained via this method are suitable for real-time simulation, data analysis, and other computational purposes requiring high-order quadrilateral meshes. To illustrate the effectiveness of the strategy, a series of experimental results are provided, demonstrating that the strategy is capable of generating high-quality meshes on a variety of complex product design domains featuring multiple domains, moving parts, holes, fillets, and other complex geometric entities. Furthermore, the strategy outperforms baseline approaches in terms of precision and efficiency. To the knowledge of the researchers, the strategy proposed, which combines optimal mesh generation, refinement, and optimization, as well as CAD-based constraint handling, represents a groundbreaking contribution to the field. The development of conversational AI requires substantial dialogue data, yet creating and collecting extensive dialogue datasets with diverse topics can be challenging. Traditional approaches to collecting data, such as online question-answer platforms, are limited by a narrow focus on specific topics. In contrast, public online forums like Reddit, with hundreds of unique topics, offer a wealth of human-written sentences for training conversational systems, although this data is often scattered and inaccessible through typical web scraping methods due to site restrictions. To effectively utilize this data, we developed LitMind, an open-source online dictionary that aggregates a large amount of Reddit text data and employs a sophisticated full-text search and question-answer system. Furthermore, we designed MindRetread, a data-scraping tool with built-in anti-block features, allowing for efficient and scalable web scraping of Reddit data. We compared the performance of our trained model using LitMind with that of MADM, a training dataset collected through manual transcription, and demonstrated LitMind's superior performance in various training tasks. Our study explores the possibilities of utilizing LitMind-derived data on a large scale and showcases its potential applications in training conversational systems with high topical diversity. The complexity of modern recommender systems forces users to make a recommendation in a short period, often with limited insight into the decision-making process. Transparent explanations can improve the user experience by providing a logical reason for each suggestion. Standard methods for generating transparent explanations, like LIME, have drawbacks. They often require a substantial computation time and don't guarantee a logical reason in all cases. This paper introduces a new approach that addresses these issues. The proposed approach, named LIME-RS, offers a logic-based ground reason for each suggestion in a timely manner. The evaluation shows that LIME-RS outperforms other explanation-based methods in terms of explanation coherence and user satisfaction. Moreover, LIME-RS offers improved overall performance in recommender systems compared to other methods. The study also highlights the importance of explaining 'not recommended' items, and this new approach makes it possible by achieving consistency with the recommender system. The experimental results demonstrate that this consistency, known as "what's excluded?", enhances user satisfaction. The authors provide a real-world case study involving movie recommendations to illustrate the benefits of the LIME-RS approach. This paper introduces an innovative method for generating synthetic speech duration
models based on medians instead of means. The median option is particularly suited
for data sets that include outliers, as it is less influenced by them. We compared
two versions of the median-based approach: a straightforward implementation and
another that incorporates an interpolation technique to deal with potential gaps
in the data. As a benchmark, we also compared these to the traditional mean-based
method. Our evaluation covered three data sets from the AMI, LJSpeech, and IBM
datasets. Overall, the results show that the median-based approach is a viable
alternative to the traditional mean-based method for duration modelling. It offers
the benefit of being resistant to outliers and allowing for handling data ranges
that are not represented in the model. In terms of performance, it tends to be no
worse and sometimes better than the mean-based approach. We also found that the
interpolation technique did not provide sufficient explanation for the observed
differences in performance. Therefore, further research is recommended to gain a
deeper understanding of the observed results. The proposed duration models were
combined with a text-to-speech system, and the output can be listened to online.  The code used in this research is available at

Identifying and analyzing online hate speech is a critical study in natural language processing, with significant real-world implications. Researchers have traditionally approached this topic as a classification task, but initial studies were hampered by data limitations. The current research landscape is hindered by the predominance of machine learning methods, despite the limitations of existing datasets. Our investigation addresses this issue by leveraging a unique dataset, consisting of 10,159 Indian comments, to explore the effectiveness of a wrapped feature selection approach in hate speech identification. The results demonstrate that feature selection can be a dependable alternative to deep learning methods, producing comparable or superior outcomes with significantly reduced computational requirements. Additionally, our research highlights the need for further data collection and showcases a promising method for hate speech identification. The associated code and data can be accessed via the link https://doi.org/10.6084/m1ci.22.1.1. Furthermore, our work has been registered on arXiv with the ID arX2.ố.0252. and on ICASSP with the ID 8011158.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate network components in parallel and combining their predictions. However, current MIMO methods where features are shared across sub-networks often hinder individual network performance. In this work, we investigate the efficacy of sequential feature sharing, an innovative MIMO framework, which allows networks to extract features independently and then align them spatially through a shared feature layer. We empirically demonstrate that sequential feature sharing enhances both overall ensemble performance and individual network predictability. Moreover, as a result of improved feature alignment, the latent space of companion networks converges towards the primary network's feature space. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that sequential feature sharing's benefits are consistent across diverse network architectures and datasets. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexk165/sequential-feature-sharing. Our findings suggest that future research should focus on designing novel MIMO architectures that facilitate independent feature extraction and spatial alignment. The insights from our study may also contribute to understanding the theoretical underpinnings of multi-network ensembles. We have identified a research gap in the MIMO community, where there is a lack of investigation into spatially coherent feature learning in ensembles. The computational advantages afforded by having multiple networks that learn together should be further explored. The variant of the sequential feature sharing framework known as $S^3$ is presented, where sub-networks' feature spaces are learned in tandem. We have also revisited current explanations for ensemble performance improvements, aiming to make these theories more precise. Overseeing industrial robots is crucial to ensuring productivity and precision. This study introduces a cutting-edge control approach that enhances position accuracy by leveraging additional sensors in the robot's joints. By implementing a set of derivative feedback controllers in conjunction with secondary encoders and a primary measurement, the proposed scheme achieves notable improvements in position stability, particularly under dynamic conditions or when the primary measurement is compromised, whether due to malfunction or typical positional errors. This configuration simplifies design, as it reduces reliance on complicated models and allows for robust performance characteristics to be derived through a method of flatness differentiation. The researchers tested the proposed regulation method on a six-axis painting robot and found that it not only augmented the robot's position accuracy but also diminished the impact of dynamic fluctuations. This innovative control approach is suitable for a broad range of applications and can be easily adapted for use on other robots. The researchers advocate for the adoption of this technique in modern industrial robots to achieve seamless and accurate movement. The study's experimental findings, which included data on the effect of dynamic shocks on the painting robot, underscored the need for refined position control in high-dynamic-content applications. This research may serve as a foundation for the development of more sophisticated algorithms to improve robot accuracy and operation. The method's open-source nature means it can be used as a model for developing new control techniques. The study's findings were presented at the 2019 IEEE International Conference on Industrial Technology. The painting robot used in these experiments is owned by the company AUBO Robotics. The researchers' novel position control approach overcomes common issues with tracking based on a single measurement, and when combined with the enhanced stability and accuracy provided by secondary encoders on the actuated axes, the resulting model is both simplified and improved, yielding similar results in both simulation and real testing. The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has been extensively researched, with a key method involving the analysis of medical history data to understand the progression of a condition. An improved analytical technique aims to provide deeper multidimensional insights into how each patient's health trajectory compares to the collective experience of all patients. To achieve this, the concept of'multiple state examination' is applied, enabling the simultaneous examination of multiple risk factors related to a condition's onset. An advanced statistical model is developed to investigate the link between these factors and the likelihood of a condition developing, taking into account factors that predict a condition will not develop as well as those that increase risk. The study demonstrates the application of this method to data from a study following patients who had a heart attack, to gain a better understanding of how factors like physical activity, body mass index, and blood pressure in different life stages influence the risk of having a heart attack. An observed relationship found that as life stage progresses, higher levels of certain factors become more strongly associated with increased risk, while others demonstrate a U-shaped relationship with increased risk, with certain values in different life stages correlating with higher risk. These findings highlight the importance of considering multiple risk factors across an individual's lifetime to develop effective prevention strategies for heart attacks. Methodologically, the study demonstrates the value of conducting multiple state examinations to explore how risk factors interact with each other throughout an individual's lifetime and influence the risk of a condition developing. Importantly, the analysis also reveals how different risk factors across life stages impact the likelihood of a condition developing for specific subgroups within a population. The developed model is theoretically valued at $0.12 per person-year, providing effective use of this analysis in public health policy making. The study data spans 1965-2011 and the analysis was completed in 2019. The findings of this study provide novel insights into how risk factors interact with each other across an individual's lifetime and influence the risk of a condition developing. The study's results have significant implications for heart attack prevention and the development of effective strategies should start as early as childhood to be most effective. Research on the molecular continuum has traditionally been characterized by an inherent dichotomy between quantum mechanical and classical approaches. However, in order to accurately model complex condensates and their interactions with matter, as well as their ability to release energy through electron transfer, a more comprehensive methodology is needed. We develop a multi-center scheme centered around an atom or molecular structure, its surroundings, and related solvent clusters, to determine the electronic environment of its core. When the QM region exceeds a certain threshold, it's necessary to enforce Pauli exclusion principles among solvent orbitals, which is also essential for validating approximate density functional linear response theories for phase transitions. We present theoretical underpinnings of our approach, illustrate its application with several examples, and compare its performance with existing methods based on density functional theory and Hartree-Fock methods. We also outline its potential extensions, including adaptations for non-adiabatic simulations and the development of a time-dependent solvent model. We show that our strategy not only provides a framework for validating approximations but also offers systematic guidelines for improving them. We also establish that our approach can be adapted for even more complex simulations in additional theoretical and computational articles. This theory is constructed by imposing a truthfulness constraint on twistor fields and their conjugates. By applying the BRST quantization, this truthfulness constraint becomes a boundary condition in the Lagrangian density. As a result, the twistor field and its conjugate have the properties of creations in the type A self-dual Yang-Mills theory. Subsequently, this approach is generalized to the type A BF theory, resulting in the creation operators for twistor fields corresponding to gluons and anti-self-dual gluons. Furthermore, combining the Zinoviev and type A BF actions, we derive the twistor action for the type A Yang-Mills theory in four-dimensional Minkowski space. Using the twistor action, we have re-expressed the partition function of the type A self-dual Yang-Mills theory in terms of twistor field creations. This re-expression reveals that the partition function can be represented as a Gaussian integral of twistor field creations and cancellations. Similarly, the partition function of the type A BF theory can also be expressed as a Gaussian integral of twistor field creations and cancellations, corresponding to gluons and anti-self-dual gluons. The application of deep learning models in medical image classification has shown significant promise due to their high degree of flexibility and the extensive range of pre-labeled medical image datasets readily available. Despite this potential, the models often perform poorly in real-world medical image classification tasks due to the presence of noisy labels. These errors can occur either intentionally, such as during the labeling process, or naturally, due to discrepancies between image descriptions and actual clinical requirements. Furthermore, the common approach of using supervised learning using cross-entropy can exacerbate the problem by favoring image-class label correlations over image-content-reflecting class relations. To address this challenge, we propose an enhanced mechanism involving label rejuvenation that leverages Bayesian statistics. By combining robust supervised learning with consistent statistical regularisation, the method ensures that the learned model accurately represents the underlying true data distribution. We test the label rejuvenation approach on both synthetic and actual datasets, yielding a notable improvement in performance, specifically an increased accuracy rate of 21.5% and 14.4% for synthetic and actual datasets, respectively. Evaluation experiments indicate that the label rejuvenation approach not only surpasses established methods in handling noisy labels but also compares favorably to a model trained on clean data. Moreover, the study highlights the importance of data quality, in particular, label reliability, in order to establish a strong foundation for training deep learning models in medical image classification tasks. The source code is accessible via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/akeshavarzian/Label-Rejuvenation-Bayesian-statistics. The medical image dataset used for the study can be found at https://www.medimtech.org.uk/datasets/. The implemented framework also enables other researchers to adapt the label rejuvenation approach to a broader range of datasets and training models. Moreover, the study has important implications beyond the scope of machine learning, in particular, highlighting the need to adopt precise algorithms for automated image analysis in medical practice. To this end, a new medical image analysis platform, named MIA4ALL, is presented, which offers an user-friendly interface to train deep learning models, thereby promoting advancement in medical AI systems. The source code is accessible via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/kesleru/MIA4ALL. The medical image analysis platform also enables other researchers to adapt the model training process to a broader dataset and provides a potential solution to develop medical AI systems that can be deployed in real-world medical settings. We investigate a modified Skyrme model incorporating infant terms alongside Born-Infeld electrodynamics, exhibiting self-dual properties. The three-dimensional soliton structure is examined, along with its corresponding electric and magnetic fields, which display regular behavior on the dark disk and tend towards vacuum at the edge. Furthermore, we explore how the soliton profile is influenced by gauge invariance effects and infra-red divergences. In addition, we determine key properties such as the magnetic flux, energy, and baryon number, in addition to analyzing quasi-topological quantities. The model also possesses quasi-topological invariants which do not depend on the choice of gauge but rather the geometric configuration of the fields. The existence of self-dual solutions indicates that these quasi-topological invariants are stable. The underlying theory is also extended to include higher-order derivatives in the Lagrangian. Although this expansion leads to a lack of self-duality within the model, we are still able to determine stable configurations on the dark disk with fields that asymptotically tend towards vacuum at the edge. In order to calculate the energy and baryon number, we are required to truncate the Lagrangian at a specified order of approximation. Within this truncated Lagrangian, we discover that the electric field contributes positively to the energy while the magnetic field and kinetic terms contribute negatively. Consequently, the total energy is determined by the balance between these competing effects. Similarly, the baryon number is found to be solely dependent on the topological magnetic field. Consequently, its sign is determined by the orientation of the magnetic field while its magnitude is determined by the intensity of the magnetic configuration. Calculations for various orders of approximation are presented in order to illustrate the interplay between electric and magnetic contributions to energy and baryon number. In addition to these numerical calculations, we are able to establish a limiting condition such that when the magnitude of the magnetic field is less than or equal to one fifth of the electrostatic potential, the energy is predominantly contributed by the electric field. Conversely, when the magnetic field is greater than one fifth of the electrostatic potential, the energy is predominantly contributed by the magnetic and kinetic terms. Utilizing these established criteria in conjunction with our previously derived equations allows for the calculation of energy and baryon number at all orders of approximation. Consequently, our work demonstrates the existence of stable, compact, energy and baryon dense configurations, amenable to numerical analysis. A key characteristic of chiral Weyl semimetals is their spontaneous breaking of time-reversal symmetry, resulting in separate Weyl cones in momentum space for spin up and spin down directions. When an external torque is applied, these cones start closing and may eventually collapse at specific momentum points, known as Weyl points, where protected topological invariants are located. In this study, researchers investigate the effect of a strong periodic electric field on a time-reversal broken Weyl semimetal in two dimensions. They show that this constant torque is equivalent to moving both the Weyl cones through a symmetric, lattice-driven pattern as the electric field is varied. The Weyl cones start folding as the electric field's intensity reaches a certain multiple of the Landau level spacing, becoming intricate, nested structures at half-integer Landau levels. The location and size of this nested structure's central, four-dimensional volume are calculated analytically and found to be directly related to key parameters and an in-plane magnetic length. Moreover, researchers demonstrate that this complex phase preserves key characteristics of time-reversal broken Weyl metals, including in-plane conductivity and a pseudospin polarization. The findings suggest that time-reversal symmetry can be broken again in this scenario, arising from charge and spin responses that exhibit spatial and temporal correlations. The investigation also highlights the coexistence of multiple time-reversal symmetry-breaking operations in this system. The study provides insights into the behavior of time-reversal broken Weyl semimetals under strong periodic electric fields and opens up possibilities for modeling materials with both time-reversal symmetry breaking and artificial magnetotransport phenomena. The researchers also discuss the applicability of their results to real-world materials like Weyl semimetal TaAs under an intense laser beam. The study provides fundamental understanding of the Hofstadter-Weyl metal in terms of its charge response, spin dynamics, and transport properties in the presence of symmetry-breaking operations in a two-dimensional setting for any integer or half integer Landau level spacing. The dependence of this complex phase on a combination of lattice and magnetic lengths is explored through the analytical solution for its central point and a scaling law for its overall size. The study provides a model to explain pseudospin polarization in this system and a transport model that explains time-reversal symmetry breaking. The researchers demonstrate that time-reversal symmetry is broken again in this model and leaves room for further symmetry operations in a time-reversal broken Hofstadter metal

The designed optical nanoantenna may also serve as a foundation for future development of various photonic components and emitters.
