This research explores how decoration with manganese influences the electronic properties of silicene, particularly when layered on hexagonal boron nitride. Employing density functional theory, we analyzed the structural and electronic features of manganese-decorated silicene and found that manganese integration leads to a minimal internal strain in silicene. Our findings also indicate that manganese has a partial positive charge when situated in the center and full negative charge at the edges of the hexagon. Based on the results from sublattice-dependent tight-binding models, we analyzed the silicene band structure in detail and discovered that manganese decoration alters the electronic properties of silicene, particularly in the presence of rippling and edge effects. These modifications render silicene suitable for application in transparent electronics. Furthermore, we investigated the interaction between manganese-decorated silicene and hexagonal boron nitride and found that a van der Waals gap forms at the interface. Our analysis also reveals potential scavenging states in boron nitride in response to manganese decoration, thereby limiting high-edge charge accumulation in silicene. These results align with existing experimental findings and provide valuable insights into the development of advanced transparent electronics. The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, is thought to be either a type Ia or a young core-collapse supernova. If it's a type Ia supernova, it would imply an unusually massive ancient black hole residing within the galaxy's center, which contradicts current observations. On the other hand, a core-collapse origin is consistent with the presence of a relatively modest, $4.2\times 10^6 M_{\odot}$, black hole at the galaxy's center, so researchers have primarily pursued this line of research. Data oversampling has long been a key technique in addressing imbalanced data sets.
We investigated eight oversampling methods designed to enhance learning with highly
imbalanced data, with a specific focus on text classification. We explored these
methods' performance under different learning paradigm conditions (boostrapping vs.
sampling) and examined the effectiveness of two. Ultimately, our analysis led us
to propose a new method called WordReptile which outperformed the other seven
methods in our experiments and showcases the potential of oversampling in text
classification tasks. We provide a thorough review of the underlying concepts
and methods, along with detailed experimental results documenting our findings. 

Note: The code used for our research has been made available on GitHub at
https://github.com/kraxigrl/oversampling-text-classification. 

Key Words: data oversampling, text classification, imbalanced data, boostrapping,
sampling, WordReptile method.

This study analyzes the relationship between local news coverage and COVID case and death rates in the United States, considering the perspective of local news audiences. It utilizes a dataset of more than 16,000 articles from 244 cities, and a geographically diverse sample of over 3,000 local news viewers. By employing hierarchical linear models, the research finds connections between COVID coverage and local case and death rates, yet these associations diminish when accounting for audience characteristics. Notably, the study reveals that communities relying on local news are associated with higher COVID case and death rates. These findings hold even after controlling for socioeconomic factors and infection rates. The research also indicates that local news viewers in cities with predominantly Democratic or Republican audiences receive different amounts of COVID coverage. Moreover, the study highlights variations in the topic focus of local news and suggests that different audience characteristics influence what local news viewers are informed about. Ultimately, the research emphasizes the impact of local news audiences on the local response to public health crises. The study's findings and data are accessible through supplementary materials. While the focus is on local news and COVID, the research's methods can be applied to a broader range of topics to facilitate future investigations. Specifically, future research could explore connections between local news coverage of social justice issues and protests, as well as the relationship between weather news and viewers' perceptions and preparations for severe weather. By utilizing a similar approach, future studies can assess the links between local news and public attitudes and behaviors on a variety of topics. The research's key findings and code for replication are provided in the online supplements. The study's conclusions were discussed at the July 2022 ELSNET conference. Simulation of fluid flow with significant angular momentum requires preserving the total amount of angular momentum.  Failing to do this causes the total angular momentum to change over time. Previously developed finite difference methods ensure that conservation of angular momentum.  However, a widely used method to speed up these simulations, known as fast multipole method, doesn't guarantee conservation of angular momentum.  We discovered that the reason for this non-conservation isn't just that the fast multipole method omits angular momentum in calculations, but also how the remaining terms are approximated.  We developed a new algorithm that ensures conservation of angular momentum by preserving the velocity field when transferring angular momentum between grid points using the fast multipole method.  By doing this, we achieved total angular momentum preservation in test cases.  The test results also show that our method is as efficient as a previously used method known as conservative smoothing.  The algorithm has been incorporated into an open-source code called OpenFOAM.  We've demonstrated its effectiveness in simulating swirling flows in a pipe with Gaussian distributions of velocity and vorticity.  The results match previously published data for circular flows and reveal previously unknown behavior of these types of flows at both the physical and numerical levels.  Furthermore, the method has also ensured total momentum conservation in incompressible fluid flow simulations.  The algorithm's implementation can be found in the commit https://gitlab.com/andywang123/astga/-/merge/3/merge.  A video demonstrating these results is at http://mnemogiakakis.com/Testing%20and%20Testing/Testing.html.  The OpenFOAM implementation is at https://github.com/OpenFOAM/main-6/pull/83606. Teaching machines how to learn is a highly valued skill that the machines
themselves possess when well-trained. Currently, the primary approach to
this skill involves providing the learner with numerous examples, a process
that is resource-intensive in terms of time and data. To improve the
efficiency of this process, we have developed a more streamlined method
that involves augmenting the learner with valuable knowledge from experienced
experts in a more condensed form. The new skill that the machines teach each
other, called expert0, efficiently distills the experts' knowledge into a more
useful format. The learner is presented with adjusted versions of its input
data, generated by manipulating the previous steps taken by expert0. To achieve
this, we have employed a sequential transformer model trained to imitate the
steps of the experts, allowing the learner to explore these steps in a more
efficient order when needed. The new method was tested on various scenarios and
demonstrated better results, particularly in terms of data efficiency, at lower
 computational complexity when compared to the traditional approach. The code
used for this experiment is publicly available at https://github.com/andreabanci/expert0.

A study of the search for two Higgs bosons created in conjunction with a vector boson has been conducted. Utilizing collision data collected at 13 TeV by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012, 2015-2018, a thorough examination of the Higgs-Vector Boson scenario is performed. This scenario, characterized by the creation of either $HHZ$ or $HHW$ or $HH$\(\gamma\)$ events, is explored under various theories including both strong and weak production mechanisms. Considering the dominant creation of events via gluon fusion for the Higgs bosons, the research examines Higgs pair production mechanisms such as gluon fusion, top-quark pairing annihilation, and weak production through W boson pairs. After evaluating the control and validation of different event signatures including all Higgs-Vector Boson, $Z$H, and $\gamma$H candidates, the research concludes that no significant deviation from the Standard Model expectations was observed in any of the analyzed channels. Consequently, the 95% confidence upper limit for the dominant Higgs pair production through the Standard Model was determined to be at least 0.0056 times the Standard Model cross-section for this scenario, depending on the Higgs boson transverse momentum. This research also enables the model interpretation of the results in various theoretical Higgs-Vector Boson scenarios. For instance, the research confirms that the Higgs-Vector Boson theory with a Higgs boson doublet mass of 700 GeV and a 100% leptophobic interaction is ruled out at 95% confidence. Our approach combines the second-order Newton method with the distributed stochastic gradient technique, creating a scalable, communication-efficient, and computationally balanced solution. To address this challenge, we developed a quantitative finite sampling accuracy guarantee, and our numerical experiments demonstrate that stochastic NAD yields significant performance enhancements over both stochastic gradient descent and a parallel Newton method, especially in cases with infrequent finite sampling. Moreover, we demonstrate that stochastic NAD satisfies a quantitative double stochastic averaging property. Building on this result and under a data stationarity assumption, we establish a finite sampling rate that guarantees convergence, effectively quantifying the trade-off between communication frequency and convergence speed. Our experimental findings also highlight the convergence speed benefits of stochastic NAD under specific data characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate numerically that stochastic NAD's performance under stochastic sampling approaches that of parallel Newton methods. The results of our numerical experiments support the validity of our convergence speed findings for stochastic NAD. This study investigates the application of machine learning algorithms in detecting hate-speech on social media platforms written in Hindi and Bengali languages. These languages are increasingly gaining prominence on online social networks, particularly among youth in India and neighboring countries. However, social media is often exploited as a means of cyberbullying and launching hate campaigns. An experimental dataset consisting of 15,000 posts was compiled from Facebook and Twitter platforms and annotated by native speakers to differentiate hate-speech as either "severe" or "mild." The findings reveal that neural networks applied with appropriate word and sentence encoding can accurately classify hate-speech with high precision and recall. Additionally, the research demonstrates that annotated datasets can be used to train an unsupervised word embedding similar to word2vec. However, it was observed that word embeddings with small training datasets can sometimes yield negative correlations between words. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of encoding when performing sentiment analysis using recurrent neural networks. An intriguing discovery was made, showing that word embeddings trained on "severe" hate-speech can effectively identify hate-speech in other languages, while also revealing that word embeddings trained on "minor offenses" fail to accurately classify "severe" hate-speech. Ultimately, the study concludes that neural networks can successfully identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali languages and discusses the challenges and future directions for researchers in natural language processing. An implementation of the method can be accessed at https://github.com/amitofir/hate-speech-ssl.

In high-stability operations of large-volume Time Projection Chambers under low-intensity conditions, signal response to single and ionized charges can be contrasted. This distinction is essential in accurately reproducing the track trajectory and identifying isotropic particle emission from nuclear reactions, particularly in scenarios involving low-recoil energies. This is especially important for future low-luminosity beam-experiments and studies of dark matter targeting detectable signals at depths involving overburden coverage. This investigation is categorically theoretical and focuses on the distinctions between two types of measurements -amplitude and area, affecting chamber performance in terms of single-ionization and recoil discrimination properties. A new set of parameters based on these measurements is introduced to boost recoil detection sensitivity. This is achieved through surface charge distribution integration and a specialized filter integrating both charge and wire collection dynamics. Results indicate that area and amplitude filters produce the most significant discrimination improvement. Furthermore, experimental data obtained from an existing TPCh named MaRTE at LNF, aimed at studying pre-amplifier gain saturation, is used to demonstrate filter utilization and determine optimization requirements. The search for close neighbors in high-dimensional data poses significant challenges in many applications, particularly when dealing with time series under the Frechet distance. This issue arises due to the distance-based method's inherent curse of dimensionality, which often results in an exponential search space. Various techniques have been developed to mitigate this problem, such as simplifications, approximations, and dimensionality reductions. However, the question of whether there are any partially metric subspaces that can support efficient searches remains open. This study addresses this question by providing tight bounds for approximate close neighbor search in time series under the Frechet distance. We show that a time series of length L and maximum derivative M can be mapped to a space with a L/M-dimensional p-metric, allowing for efficient query processing using a time-efficient algorithm. Additionally, we propose an algorithm to efficiently find close neighbors in a time-series database. This database is assumed to be preprocessed using a k-means algorithm, which groups time series into cluster centers using approximate distances based on a user-specified parameter ε. The algorithm first determines the most relevant cluster for a given query time series and finds two time series in that cluster that serve as bounds for the query's close neighbors. The algorithm achieves this by utilizing a novel method for online approximation of distances and applying it to find the most similar time series to a query time series in a cluster. The method first approximates a query time series to a single point and then uses this point to match the ends of a query time series with the ends of other time series in a cluster. The algorithm then iteratively refines its search for the closest time series by narrowing down its search space. The method achieves a time complexity of O(L^(2+ε/((L/M)^p))) for approximating a query time series, as well as for finding its closest time series to a query time series. The algorithms' performance is validated through a comparison with the time-series classifier System-C from the literature, which claims to outperform other state-of-the-art algorithms. In various fields such as quantum information, advanced materials characterization and light sources measurement, pioneering techniques necessitate error correction due to limitations in measurement instruments. Techniques like maximum likelihood unfolding utilize Bayesian methods to correct measurement distortions, which become increasingly demanding computationally as data volumes increase. Novel applications often require optimizing these methods as well. We introduce a versatile, iterative Bayesian unfolding framework addressing these issues, by leveraging a unified Priestly transformation model, allowing for model assessment and priors development. Our method enhances MLE performance, provides robust model robustness and reliable uncertainty quantification, all while utilizing vectorized and Cox-Krall sampling methods for increased efficiency. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical comparison with existing methods as well as a real-world application involving cutting-edge photonics time-resolved measurements. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/andreaborella/SCUBEU.

As robots prepared to integrate into daily life, their ability to function alongside humans depend on the standards they establish for cooperative interactions.
A significant obstacle preventing widespread deployment of autonomous systems stems from inconsistent and limited interactions with humans, often dictated by bespoke solutions designed by the company providing the system.
A key limitation hindering advanced systems, particularly those employing autonomous systems, is their inability to effectively engage with unskilled individuals who may encounter obstacles.
To address these concerns, we developed an autonomous system that adjusts its behavior in response to the attitude displayed by a human interacting with it in a shared environment.
A major breakthrough was achieved by recognizing that human cooperation with the system could be represented through a sequence of preferred system behaviors.
By applying statistical analysis to the interactions of multiple individuals, we discovered a set of universal, descriptive elements that could be used to create a language model.
Our model enables a shared autonomous system to anticipate and adapt to various human interactions in diverse scenarios, thus enhancing user experience and empathy.
Ultimately, it is anticipated that establishing a common, structured language could facilitate the development of a unified standard for collaborative interactions between humans and autonomous systems, paving the way for seamless and efficient interactions in real-world environments.

This discrepancy can lead to different model performance even when trained on similar data. To address this concern, we developed a Federal Learning framework that allows existing models to adapt to new hospitals while maintaining its original performance. This federal model then trains on clinical data from a new hospital, and we observed that it achieves comparable results which are similar to re-training the model from scratch on that hospital's data. Moreover, the federal model's performance exhibits a correlation with the similarity in data, and this similarity can be quantified using the Multivariate Normal Mixtures (MNM) measure. By analyzing pressure as a function of packing density, they were able to identify unique phases that arise due to the presence of these non-spherical particles. Beyond the established face-centered cubic and body-centered tetragonal structures found in systems of hard spheres, additional crystalline phases emerged, characterized by the presence of modulated splay order in the middle layer and a combination of hexagonal and tetragonal configurations in the outer layers. These middle-layer phases occurred across a wide range of temperatures and pressures and were found in conjunction with both the plastic hexagonal crystal and the body-centered tetragonal crystal structure. For specific temperature and pressure conditions, a middle-layer phase coexisting with the liquid and the plastic hexagonal crystal was observed. In addition, researchers discovered a unique outer-layer configuration featuring hexagonal and tetragonal arrangements, which was found under high pressure conditions and is known as the HBT phase. This phase coexists with the liquid crystal and the plastic hexagonal crystal, with further analysis via the second-order virial coefficients indicating that the HBT phase is likely stabilized by specific two-body interactions. Paired-learning models, which combine partial-reward learning with contextual information, have achieved impressive results in robot task instructions.  This study examines the task of assembling objects by following verbal instructions and explores the importance of the contextual component.  It compares the performance of a paired-likelihood model, which updates rules and object configurations based on observational data, to a model that omits contextual information and solely relies on rule-preference learning.  To evaluate the paired model's reliance on contextual data, a variant that excludes contextual information is introduced, replacing it with pre-defined rules.  When contextual information is provided, the paired model significantly outperforms its non-contextual counterpart.  However, the paired model's performance suffers when contextual information is hidden, indicating that the majority of task benefits derive from the rule-update aspect rather than the contextual component.  These findings underscore the need to discern when contextual information is pivotal in enhancing paired-learning models' task-solving capabilities. Importantly, our research demonstrates the applicability of the relative-entropy and relative-configurational enthalpy schemes that were originally developed for studying amorphous solids to the study of polymer liquids that are relevant to many practical applications. When generating output in neural machine translation, the current token is typically the main focus. However, we propose deviating from this standard focus on a token-by-token basis to instead prioritize future tokens, which we believe to be more inherently relevant in a translation task. By doing so, we expect a better alignment with the source side, which would lead to improved translations. Two methods - one relying on an additional trainable model and another on a pre-trained NMT model's attention distribution - were explored to determine ahead-looking focal points. These methods can be integrated with virtually any neural machine translation model without significant computational overhead. Experimental results show that our proposed approach yields consistent translation enhancements across models of different sizes and varieties, as well as in cases with increased source-side context words. Notably, we observed up to 3.24 BLEU score improvements on the NIST Chinese-to-English dataset without any enhancements to the optimizer or training data. Moreover, we found that certain models were less accurate but could still match the translation quality of top models when trained to a higher level of perfection. Overall, our results suggest that a strategy prioritizing future output tokens in neural machine translation can bring significant translation improvements to established models with minimal computational costs. Such an approach is particularly beneficial for translations requiring extended context, such as summaries, which often result in more challenging translation tasks. A simplified yet effective variation of this strategy - simply shifting the focus one token ahead on a token-by-token basis - was also found to have a negligible yet positive impact on translation accuracy. Further analysis revealed that our proposed method's effectiveness can be attributed to a better alignment with the source side, which we observed in models focusing ahead but not necessarily those focusing ahead by multiple tokens. Notably, while focusing ahead by multiple tokens allows for a better source-to-target alignment, it also leads to an overly narrow focus on the translation task. Hence, finding an optimal balance between past and future focal points is crucial for top-performing translations, which we were able to achieve with our proposed simple yet effective approach. Human evaluations also confirmed the advantages of our proposed method, as translations obtained with this strategy received higher scores and were deemed more coherent and fluent. Thus, our research demonstrates the value of an adaptable focus that can be adjusted to accommodate both past and future output tokens to yield superior neural machine translation results. The universe's gamma-ray emission is observed as a background pattern, derived from various astronomical sources including galaxies, the cosmic microwave background, and cosmic rays. Observations indicate that gamma-rays emanating from galaxy clusters are dispersed and are found to exceed predictions based on the synchrotron radiation of cosmic rays interacting with magnetic fields, a phenomenon known as the "excess diffuse gamma-ray background." Studies of a dozen clusters have provided data on their gamma-ray emission. Recent studies aimed to understand Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have exposed their tendency to focus on irrelevant details in image classification tasks. To address this issue, we introduce LVFF, a novel explanatory framework that combines visual and semantic filter representation to identify and analyze DCNN's discriminative pattern focus. LVFF utilizes a 2D hybrid attention mechanism to accurately pinpoint the focus of each filter within the original image coordinates. LVFF also achieves spatial alignment by leveraging a common coordinate framework for both the image and feature map. Furthermore, it generalizes semantic pattern focus by considering multiple labels, allowing it to reveal multiple focus patterns for each filter. Experiments conducted on CIFAR-10, ImageNet-14, and ImageNet100 datasets validate the effectiveness of LVFF in accurately detecting consistent pattern focus for individual filters and distinguishing between discriminative and non-discriminative filter patterns. Building upon LVFF, we develop a novel feature-based discriminative filter identification method that surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches by achieving a higher accuracy rate of 84.95% on CIFAR-10 and 89.23% on ImageNet-14. LVFF also facilitates evaluation and comparison of feature learning strategies and their practical applications in adversarial robustness, and also investigates the effectiveness of transfer learning for small-scale datasets like CIFAR-10. High-dimensional dynamic variable models, which include conditional models and
hierarchical models like LSTMs and their state-space counterparts, are widely used
for analyzing time series data despite limitations in handling nonlinear
correlations, discontinuities in data and non-stationarity. This review focuses
on practical aspects of applied research in this field, including state space
models, their variants such as LSTMs, multiplicative models, latent variable models
and dynamic cluster models. These models are utilized in various real-world
scenarios to address questions in the fields of economics, medicine, and
environmental science. This review aims to provide an in-depth understanding
of the concepts and methods involved, allowing readers to critically evaluate
the underlying mathematics and choose the most suitable approach for their own
research. As an example, this review presents a comprehensive analysis of the
medical application of multi-variable dynamic cluster models for identifying
disease patterns. Following a concise introduction, the chapters delve into the
underlying theory and implementation of each model type, starting with conditional
models, then exploring hierarchical models, before concluding with practical
considerations and suggestions for future research directions. Finally, this
review highlights the broad range of real-world applications for high-dimensional
dynamic variable models, from identifying nonlinear system patterns to estimating
non-stationary probability distributions over extended periods. One promising
area for further research lies in the use of state-space models that incorporate
latent variables. This approach not only offers a flexible framework for high
dimensional time series analysis but also lends itself to efficient model selection
and identification of the underlying dynamics. By leveraging LSTMs, researchers can
investigate the local structure of state-space models on a variable-by-variable
basis, effectively turning the model identification problem into a dimensionality
reduction task. Given the vast applications across fields, this review concludes
by suggesting that high-dimensional dynamic variable models remain a vital tool
for interdisciplinary research in the social and natural sciences. As such, future
researchers should continue developing and refining this tool, exploring new
applications and leveraging advanced methodologies to stay at the forefront of
the intersection of statistical modeling, machine learning and data analysis. The
corresponding software, including the R packages mdcmR, mdcmNomletR, dynamo, dynamoMed, dynamoEcon and dynamoEnv, along with the condModZ R package, are publicly available and complement this review. The associated condModZ R packages -- dynamo, dynamoMed

The calculation of atomic physics interactions in exotic atoms is inherently complicated. When considering real-world applications of such calculations, factors become even more intricate. For instance, when determining an atom's interaction with various materials, the finite depth of the potential well must be accounted for, necessitating numerical solutions to complex equations. An innovative approach to calculating one-dimensional Schrödinger equations has been developed, specifically tailored for dimuonium-atom interactions in different substances. This method employs the finite difference method, utilizing a precomputed lookup table to solve for energy levels accurately and efficiently. Key parameters such as energy gaps and wave function values at specific points are calculated and presented, offering valuable insights into exotic atom behavior. An overview of MuMuPy, a Python-based software tool for performing these calculations, is provided, along with a demonstration of its capabilities through a selection of case studies. These case studies examine the interactions between dimuonium and substances like hydrogen, deuterium, helium, and carbon dioxide, highlighting patterns and relationships among the results. By facilitating a deeper understanding of the unique properties observed in exotic atoms, this software serves as a valuable resource for further research in the field. Their research showed that several Thompson's groups have infinite divergence. Building on Golan and Sapir's findings, we introduce new inequalities for metric-type functions, and prove that many Thompson's groups and their braided versions have unique metrics where the distance between elements is directly proportional to the least number of braids required to map one element to the other. We also demonstrate that some subsets of these groups, similar to right-associative braided-Thompson's groups, have bounded displacement with respect to their metrics. We further demonstrate that right-associative braided-Thompson's groups have a consistent consistent uniform bounded displacement. Consequently, we demonstrate the continuity of shift maps within braided-Thompson's groups. To support our continuity findings, we establish new set equivalences for the braided-Thompson's groups. Lastly, using Golan and Sapir's research on the relationship between divergence and metrics in these groups, we prove that right-associative braided-Thompson's groups have a consistent consistent divergence. As a result, the continuity and divergence findings for braided-Thompson's groups contradict previous conjectures by Golan and Sapir. Recently, a paper was published on how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models can be optimized for question and answer tasks. In this paper, we explain how our team adapted the architecture of RAG, a model composed of a document retriever and a paragraph reader, to better perform in the context of the Natural Language Inference (NLI) task. We provide a step-by-step guide detailing our approach, starting with the development of a strategy to divide datasets into training, validation sets. We successfully implemented dense retrieval using an Anki-based database to enhance model performance. We further explored using negative sampling and the effects it has on the model's performance when trained with or without. We demonstrated the effectiveness of combining the document and paragraph level representations to improve the model's performance. We examined the impact of different transformer sizes for the generator and retriever components, and how training the model on different layers affects its performance. We compared the performance of different models and found that a model trained on the full NLI dataset, using dense retrieval and negative sampling, achieved state-of-the-art results. We further tested the model's robustness by evaluating its performance on out-of-distribution tasks, including the complex multi-Hop reasoning tasks. Our results showed significant improvements across various tasks, and the code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/allenai/fine-tune-rag-nli. A central concern when delegating micro-tasks to crowds involves identifying and engaging competent participants. Research has proposed various approaches for determining worker qualifications, yet studies examining the practicality of these methods under real-world crowdsourcing conditions are scarce. In this research, we investigate the effectiveness of evaluation tasks in establishing worker qualifications and the influence of evaluation tasks on worker behavior. Our investigation focuses on the dynamics of worker evaluation and qualification in three distinct crowds: (1) a newly formed crowd with undefined processes, (2) a crowd where participation is voluntary and subject to change, and (3) a crowd where participation is fixed. In studying these cases, we discover that (1) initial evaluation tasks have a notable impact on worker qualification methods, (2) compensation and reliability principles can significantly affect worker behavior, and (3) propellerian crowds may offer benefits in terms of worker qualification consistency. Ultimately, our research emphasizes the importance of adapting crowdsourcing strategies to the inherent characteristics of its workers. The findings presented here provide valuable insights for practitioners and researchers on the utilization of evaluation tasks in establishing worker qualifications, in addition to offering an in-depth examination of the impact of crowdsourcing dynamics on worker behavior. Furthermore, we present "QualiaCrowd," a novel qualification system (available at https://qualicrowd.com/), which demonstrates that with a tailored approach, it is feasible to build a competent crowd over time. Our work highlights the significance of adapting crowdsourcing strategies to the unique traits of a crowd and the need to specify the mechanics of both the crowd and the tasks assigned to it. By doing so, we improve our comprehension of the crowd, facilitate transparent interactions, and establish a crowd with consistent and predictable behavior. Text clip retrieval, a crucial component of text-based visual retrieval and video analysis, is increasingly important due to rapid advancements in video generation and detection. Current best approaches rely on expensive pre-trained visual features and rely on heuristics to combine text and visual features. To address this limitation, we propose a novel end-to-end framework called TS2-Net that uses a single model to generate strong and discriminative features for both text and clip. To achieve this, we introduce a dynamic attention transformer that not only captures complex interactions between text and clip features but also allows token positions to be adaptive and correlated with the query's semantic meaning. Furthermore, we develop a dual-selection mechanism to determine which tokens and how much to take from both the text and clip features. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of TS2-Net, which surpasses the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin on both LiMuDa and RuDi datasets, while also dramatically reducing computation by at least 60% and showcasing impressive grounding capabilities. The code and models are available at https://github.com/whwu/TS2-Net.

A locally usual measure algebra is one that complies with three conditions:
The finiteness condition, similarity to the usual measure, and finite additivity. 
We have found that locally usual measure algebras consist of discrete and atomic measure algebras, probability measures on finite groups, and probability measures on finite sets with a countable basis. 
Additionally, we have established two valuation theorems for measures on finite sets with a countable basis. 
One such theorem applies to free measures, while the other covers measures with respect to a filter on the natural numbers. 
These theorems also help us determine when two locally usual measure algebras are equivalent, and we obtain a characterization of relatively atomic measure algebras in terms of free measures. 
Furthermore, we have established a Stone-type theorem for locally usual measure algebras, and as a result, we have obtained a characterization of atomic measure algebras corresponding to ultrafilters on the natural numbers. 
This characterizations also imply that every free measure corresponding to a filter has a unique completion, and that every relatively atomic measure algebra contains a unique free measure corresponding to that atom. 
Finally, we have demonstrated that the family of free measures corresponding to filters in the realm of measure algebras is well-defined and closed under taking suprema. 
This family also has an associated dual consisting of measure algebras corresponding to finitely additive ultrafilters on the natural numbers, and this duality is deep and profound. 
To further this duality, we have constructed a measure algebra corresponding to a ultrafilter on the natural numbers that does not belong to any relatively atomic measure algebra. 
This measure algebra's existence prompts the question of whether every locally usual measure algebra is relatively atomic. 
Unfortunately, this possibility remains unresolved. 
However, the measure algebra created in our example is unique in that its corresponding free measure is discrete, and thus the existence of this measure algebra raises another question - is every discrete free measure algebra locally usual? 
Once more, the answer to this question remains unknown. 
Yet, the possibility of the free measure being discrete being both necessary and sufficient for local usualness presents an intriguing idea. 
That is, if a discrete free measure were to fail in being locally usual, then the corresponding trace would fail in being finite additive. 
This would imply local finiteness is necessary for discrete measures to be locally usual. 
Ultimately, multiple questions regarding the characteristics and properties of locally usual measure algebras and their associated free measures remain unresolved

A new method is proposed for learning a deep representation of input data by optimizing a variational model based on the Sinkhorn divergence. This divergence, which generalizes the Hobbs function, has been proven effective in various applications including their use in Optimal Transport theory. Research demonstrates that existing algorithms for calculating Sinkhorn divergence struggle with large-scale datasets; as a result, a new formulation of the problem that enables end-to-end training with deep neural networks is developed. This method is then tested on a variety of data representation and dimensionality reduction tasks; in these cases, results show that learning representations optimized with the Sinkhorn divergence surpass those achieved with traditional deep neural network methods such as PCA, autoencoders, and U-Net. This new approach is shown to effectively learn representations that are adaptive to input data. Furthermore, its performance is comparable to state-of-the-art methods even when training data is limited. This approach is applied to a range of different data, including natural images, text data, and graph-based data. In response to COVID-19, a range of contact tracing efforts across various countries were quickly established to provide compensation for the limitations of official contact tracing services.  Specifically, in England, these external efforts primarily involved private sector groups using mobile technology to identify and contact individuals who had come into close contact with COVID-19 cases.  While these efforts were undertaken, there were significant uncertainties surrounding their effectiveness and impact on the overall performance of the contact tracing system.  This research aims to investigate whether the external tracing efforts, known as the National Institute of Health (NIH) Partners and the Test, Track and Trace (TTP) Additional Resources (TaR), had any effect on the performance of the contact tracing system.  By utilizing a simulation model of the COVID-19 contact tracing system, researchers were able to determine that neither NIH Partners nor TTP altered the desired performance characteristics of the system, but did result in changes to the actual system performance.  By applying a novel metric for assessing the economic value of these external tracing efforts, and utilizing their previously estimated costs and incidence rates, researchers were able to place an upper bound on their economic value.  Notably, the study found that the external tracing efforts were likely to have increased overall system transmission failure rates, and resulted in unnecessary isolation in order to compensate for their own investigative transmissions.  By eliminating the extra transmissions introduced by these external efforts, and not incurring their additional isolation costs, the study estimated that NIH Partners had an economic value of up to $\$53.8M$ and TTP had an economic value of up to $\$69.9M$.  These findings provide timely insights that could inform future COVID-19 response policies and potentially serve as a framework for assessing the impact of similar programs in uninfected systems.  Moreover, the study provides several novel contributions including the development of a model to compare to real data, the creation of new metrics to measure the performance of contact tracing efforts and their components, the application of established principles to determine their economic value, and the proposal of a time-uninfected model to simulate the effects of COVID-19 contact tracing efforts and their transmissions.  This research also offers potential extensions including the development of a model to simulate the effects of COVID-19 infections on a fixed population and the application of established principles to determine the economic value of COVID-19 contact tracing efforts and their transmissions. topological structure of these functions as complex parameters change. Our focus
is on Betti numbers in the sparse regime of Gaussian voyages, where we demonstrate
a change in the behavior of these numbers from vanishing to significant values.
Notably, our findings are validated through numerical simulations for a recently developed
Betti number estimator. Furthermore, we provide theoretical support for the behavior
of these numbers using the stochastic geometry of subsets with negligible Gaussian
measure, combined with an invariance principle for random variables characterized by
negligible Gaussian measures. Finally, an algorithmic approach is used to prove that
homology persistence offers a means to estimate the correct order of parameters
$\alpha_s$ for any $s$ in the range from 0 to 1. This order is shown to be equivalent
to the exponential rates of Betti numbers' convergence based on the Frechet derivative
of Gaussian voyages' expected values. The outcome is known as homological frequency
estimation (HFE). For instance, applying HFE with a specified hyperparameter setup
allows for the estimation of $\alpha_0$ up to an error margin of $10^{-10}$ in the
case of $n=160$ and $m=128$ for which the convergence times amount to approximately
$2.8$ and $3.8$ seconds, respectively. The implementation of HFE can be accessed at

A robotic system's ability to accurately assemble parts depends on precise placement and positioning of its tools, including cameras and grippers. While vision systems are used for detecting objects and guiding motion in assembly tasks, using a gripper camera for task planning can be complicated due to the unwelcome introduction of extraneous data and visual information, especially when there is no reliable method for easily adjusting the camera's position and orientation. To address this challenge, we propose an automated solution that uses a single image to determine the necessary adjustments to a robotic system's eye-in-hand camera, thereby minimizing unnecessary vision data and improving performance, as shown in experiments using a UR5 robot and an RGB-D camera attached to a gripper. Our proposed technique was successfully tested in a real-world assembly task, outperforming existing methods of camera calibration and task planning. In typical reinforcement learning, we specify the goals of an agent. However, in reverse reinforcement learning, we define the agent's behavior itself and instead extract a suitable reward function that the agent uses to optimise its performance. This is a difficult task because we need to achieve a consistent understanding of the desired outcomes, which becomes apparent when trying to reverse engineer the reward method with multiple possible objectives. This paper proposes a new approach that narrows down suitable outcomes by incorporating learning in both policy and reward simultaneously, using a small dataset of expert transitions to guide the process. Our model uses a representation of the reward function as a spectral density in a Gaussian process and applies variational methods to optimise both policy and reward simultaneously, keeping them in balance. This approach was successfully tested on complex tasks, including a challenging multi-step sequence of actions, a complex 3D grid-based game of tic-tac-toe, and a 3D maze-solving task. This difficulty is particularly prominent when accounting for ohmic dissipation in the system, as it amplifies the importance of tunneling resistance and contact variability. This article explores the feasibility of identifying Majorana zero-bias peaks for the first time under conditions of increased ohmic dissipation and varied contact resistance. Our research reveals that in this context, Majorana zero-bias peaks exhibit distinct temperature-dependent characteristics, relatively sharp peak shapes, and relatively lower temperature onset for their appearance, which differentiates them from other possible zero-bias peaks. These findings provide a concrete guideline to experimentally verify the presence of Majorana modes in tunneling spectroscopy. Furthermore, a novel technique involving the use of proximity-induced superconductivity near the charging energy for distinguishing between Majorana and non-topological zero-bias peaks is introduced. Our study demonstrates that for the scenario of highly resistant electrodes experiencing ohmic dissipation, a notable superconducting gap forms adjacent to the charging energy of topological modes with near-100% confidence, in contrast to non-topological modes with their corresponding values close to zero. These experimental results identify the proximity-induced superconductivity as an indispensable factor for accurately distinguishing between Majorana and non-topological zero-bias peaks under conditions of high resistance and significant dissipation. Our research delves into the underlying physics of superconducting gaps formed near the charging energies of both topological and non-topological modes for the first time, providing a clear understanding of their relationships with tunneling density of states, tunneling barrier height, and the distance between the electrodes. These experimental findings may be of value in future investigations of tunneling spectroscopy. Additionally, a new method of identifying topological modes via their unique relationships with superconducting gaps near the charging energies is presented. In domains with extensive use of ontologies, users often needs to grasp the interconnections between multiple ontologies, giving rise to newly minted ontologies with thousands of terms and hundreds of thousands of relationships. Unfortunately, the majority of visualization tools available are suited for hierarchical or time-based data. To address this disparity, OntoPlot was developed as a general-purpose visualization tool for visualizing large ontologies, specifically designed to efficiently handle non-hierarchical data. OntoPlot works by partitioning a hierarchical tree-view into multiple panels that display a selection of sub-ontologies, allowing users to dynamically adjust the size of each panel and redetermine which terms within each sub-ontology are most relevant. A new method of computing relevance has been developed, tailored to work effectively with large amounts of data, by first identifying a term's central point and then determining its proximity to other terms. A comprehensive user study involving 60 participants compared OntoPlot's usability to that of existing visualizations, namely Proteins, TabPro, and Graph, concluding that OntoPlot outperformed the control group by 22%. We introduce an novel technique for semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition that focuses on resolving inter-domain and style transformations. Inter-domain approaches aim to tackle differences between training and testing data distributions by modeling cross-domain mappings, unlike traditional methods that address domain shifts within a single domain. Our method leverages CycleGAN-based inter-domain loss to mitigate domain discrepancies in training data, alongside an inter-domain loss that models the mapping between training and testing domain distributions. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly improves the state-of-the-art speech recognition achievements on the Switchboard and VoiceTest datasets. Notably, we achieve up to 18% relative improvement over the inter-domain state-of-the-art method on the Switchboard dataset. Our findings also highlight the effectiveness of using a combination of inter-domain and intra-domain losses in inter-domain E2E ASR setups, revealing that such a combination yields improved performance compared to utilizing only intra-domain losses. Moreover, we show that our method addresses domain shifts in a scalable and computationally efficient manner, requiring only a single graphics processing unit (GPU) for training. The necessity for Automated Essay Assessment arises due to an increasing shortage of teachers and their demanding roles. Its application is restricted by computational limitations, however. A popular approach uses supervised machine learning models that recognize patterns in written language, such as logistic regression and support vector machines, or more recent transformer-based models like BERT and XLNet. The latter type has shown significant advancements in this area with its self-attention mechanism and unsupervised pre-training capabilities. This research compares the performance of BERT, XLM, and XLNet in Automated Essay Assessment tasks, including both score prediction and essay similarity assessment, using an Italian language dataset. The models were trained with speed-optimized variants of the XLM-R and a newly proposed version of XLNet, both designed to enhance efficiency while maintaining accuracy. The results show that the newly proposed model, aimed at improving computational efficiency, achieves comparable or better results in AWA tasks, using an NVIDIA V100 GPU as the computing device. A further analysis of the models' behavior in terms of computational complexity and accuracy is provided, and the findings have implications on the design of Automatic Essay Assessment models, encouraging the development of more efficient solutions that can effectively meet the demands of this area. To address the challenge of domain adaptation in pedestrian detection, we examine the role of false positives (FPs) as useful information for identifying true positives (TPs). Our research indicates that FPs with lower similarity scores between images contain more valuable box information compared to those with higher scores. Based on this insight, we develop a novel unsupervised method that employs self-supervised learning to assign similarity-dependent weights to each FP box, enhancing the contribution of low-similarity FP boxes. As a result, the detection model is stimulated to directional learning, particularly towards more TPs. We call this method Box Re-Ranking (BRR). Our experiments on benchmark datasets reveal that BRR consistently reduces the false positive rate by at least 11%, yielding a superior trade-off between the precision and recall compared to state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, our method outperforms the baseline with significant improvements on the benchmark datasets. The related code and implementation can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/IndigoPurple/Box-Re-Ranking. Our method also received an award at the ICCV 2021 Main Paper. This study explores advancements in music generation, specifically focusing on two sub-tasks: arranging multiple musical notes into a musical format, and converting musical representations into audio recordings. Building upon the success of image manipulation techniques such as image-to-image translation and style mixing, we develop a novel approach for simultaneously achieving these two sub-tasks using a single model. Our model relies on two decoder networks, one responsible for converting musical data into images and another for generating audio recordings from those images. Additionally, we introduce several techniques to improve the quality of the generated music, including methods to handle note duration, pitch ranges, and compressed music file reconstruction. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple metrics demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed method over multiple music generation benchmarks. Moreover, subjective user assessments further validate the high quality and realism of the generated music. Interestingly, our research reveals that transforming musical data into images not only enhances quantitative performance but also makes the music generation process more understandable for human reviewers. Our primary objective is to investigate how throwing motions are perceived when the point of release does not match the expected standard. To achieve this, we create artificial throwing motions by combining the grip pose at the point of release with simulations of ballistic trajectories, resulting in a different point of release than the initial grip pose. We then introduce a subjective survey that assesses both the realism of the simulated throwing motion and the perceiver's ability to identify the point of release as being incorrect. The survey's results demonstrate that the simulated throwing motions are deemed realistic and that the majority of participants struggle to accurately identify the point of release as being incorrect. Moreover, our results indicate that more accurate predictions of the point of release correspond to smaller discrepancies between the point of release and the point of peak velocity, as well as shorter throwing distances. Interestingly, our findings also reveal that the angle of the throwing motion and the timing of the peak velocity have minimal effects on the accuracy of the point of release. To advance research in the evaluation of virtual human motions, we suggest two new metrics: $\delta_{\rm PR}$ and $\delta_{\rm tR}$. The first metric measures the average difference between the predicted and actual points of release, while the second metric estimates the standard deviation of the distribution of time differences between the frames before the point of release and the frames after it. The larger the $\delta_{\rm tR}$, the smaller the expected $\delta_{\rm PR}$ and vice versa. The $\delta_{\rm tR}$ metric exhibits a more direct correlation with our realism ratings and the ability to identify the point of release as being incorrect. The proposed method provides a potential solution to generate more realistic throwing motions, particularly in scenarios where the point of release differs from the initial grip pose. In astrophysics, understanding how molecules form and break apart is crucial for explaining how certain molecules are abundant in space. Researchers have been studying the binding energy distribution of molecules by modeling interactions between atoms and small molecules, but a unified database for this information was missing. A new database, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, collects and provides access to the binding energy distributions for various astrophysical molecules, including diatomic species and molecules up to six atoms in size. To be included in the database, the binding energy distributions must be based on accurate quantum chemical calculations at zero Kelvin and meet specific criteria for consistency and precision. With over 170 binding energy distributions for different astrophysical molecules in the database, the BAP aims to provide a valuable resource for researchers to assess the plausibility of observed interstellar molecules, as well as inform modeling and simulations in astrochemistry. The database is available online at https://beap.cfa.harvard.edu/.

We explore shallow circuits produced by random Clifford gates in conjunction with partial trace output, generating shadows of unknown states. By evaluating the depth of these circuits, we identify a threshold at which the generated shadows effectively approximate minimal position-based shadows. Further investigation into this approximation yields insights into the performance variability among distinct low-depth circuits. Utilizing state-of-the-art machine learning techniques, we train models to predict expectation values from the output shadows. Our analysis shows that the impact of depth on the predictability of expectation values follows a logarithmic pattern. Additionally, we found that increasing circuit width at a constant depth leads to improved predictability. Our findings also highlight the significant influence of gate specificiness on the accuracy of expectation value predictions. Ultimately, we established that the predictive error can be reduced by leveraging the eigenvalue-based correlation among expectation values of identical gates. This error reduction effectively compensates for the negative effects associated with gate specificiness. The resources required to achieve these outcomes are within the capabilities of near-term quantum devices, making them a promising option for practical applications. The development of these algorithms brings us closer to leveraging near-term devices for a broader scope of tasks, including certain types of quantum-assisted machine learning. Moreover, trained models can facilitate the estimation of Hamiltonian matrix elements, a technique that may be used to refine measurement precision in experimental settings. The field of NLP is becoming increasingly vulnerable to adversarial attacks that exploit errors in model training data, notably in text classification. To address such data flaws, we introduce the Sibyl variant, a language model variant designed to tolerate deviations from its original training. This variant is trained on multiple, slightly altered versions of the original dataset. To generate these variations, we developed a data manipulation method that slightly alters the word embeddings of the original data. We then trained variants of BERT and RoBERTa models with these modified data sets and evaluated them using adversarial and robust accuracy metrics. Our experiments on two prominent datasets showed that our method achieves superior robust accuracy and maintains or improves standard accuracy compared to a baseline model trained on the original data. This research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/amanpreet87/Sibylvariant. Our results suggest that language model variants can effectively withstand errors in training data and may be applied to a wide array of text processing tasks. Furthermore, we found that the model's stability depends on the degree of modification, and that more significant changes may have undesirable effects on the model. This method also requires careful selection of the number of variations to introduce. We were able to achieve comparable or better accuracy on the NLI and SST2 datasets using three variations. Our research also reveals that the variant model's standard accuracy can be further enhanced by using a small amount of the original data for fine-tuning. This approach of training language model variants with multiple, slightly altered data sets is a promising method for enhancing text classification model resilience and standard accuracy in the face of dataset flaws. It is also one of the first methods to address such dataset flaws. Our research opens up new avenues of investigation, including an examination of the variant's performance on other prominent NLP datasets, an exploration of the optimal degree of modification, a more in-depth analysis of the model's local and adversarial robustness, and an assessment of methods to automatically introduce variations from existing datasets. The variant's capabilities in these areas could potentially be expanded by introducing variations not only in word embeddings but also by manipulating other data attributes such as parts-of-speech, syntactic tree structures, reference distributions, human annotations, salient points, and related concepts. This approach could lead to significant gains in various text processing tasks across multiple NLP benchmarks. The increasing prominence of meta-learning and representation learning in AI research reflects their potential to accelerate learning across diverse, previously unseen domains. Traditional approaches, however, often require extensive labeling or prior expertise, hindering their applicability in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, allowing models to freely develop domain-specific representations can result in inconsistent, often inaccurate, representations that fail to generalize. In our research, we present learnable, linear representations that can be effectively obtained both through supervised learning and self-directed, undirected learning. We demonstrate that a meta-algorithm operating within a meta-representation space, characterized by a meta-manifold, is capable of discovering and managing these linear representations across diverse domains, ultimately leading to improved generalization. Notably, this meta-algorithm is capable of recognizing and maintaining the structural similarities within these representations, even in scenarios where it encounters complex, high-dimensional data. In line with this concept, we present the T2SA framework, a novel, end-to-end, undirected learning method designed to facilitate meta-representation meta-learning. The T2SA framework incorporates novel techniques for stabilizing the meta-representation space on a geometric structure, ultimately yielding improved generalization and robustness. The T2SA framework's effectiveness is empirically validated through its successful application to various challenging, multi-domain datasets commonly employed in visual recognition tasks. Developing small language models to reduce computational costs has driven the investigation of quantization techniques and language transformation. Such methods compress models either by reducing weights to lower bit lengths or translating language from the original to a compressed form. This research compares the practical applications of these techniques in training self-attention mechanisms for a low-resource machine translation task using data from the Wikipedia's MT dataset. The study examines two approaches: training with quantized weights of varying depths and compressing the English side of the data using different compression techniques. The results show that distillation yields superiorble results in a reduction of the task's difficulty, but the advantage diminishes as the amount of training data increases. Notably, the most substantial improvements were observed at very low levels of compression and training depths. Additionally, the research explores the potential of distillation as a pre-training strategy for small MT models before conducting fine-tuning, finding that it can lead to notable improvements in cases of scarce training data. Finally, the findings suggest that distillation and quantization have synergistic effects, allowing for a substantial decrease in both the number of training parameters and the model's entropy without a notable decline in the accuracy of the translation. This outcome suggests the possibility of using distillation as a pre-training strategy for small MT models before conducting fine-tuning, particularly in scenarios where there is limited training data available. Previous solutions often relied on incorporating visual information, but this proved difficult due to the distinct natures of images and language. Our approach takes a different route by formulating image description as a text modification task. Our model, IPD, is the first to combine visual and linguistic inputs in this context. The growing integration of machine learning algorithms in diverse domains has led to concerns over a key challenge: effectively merging information from skilled domain experts and scientists and technical machine learning professionals. While experts can provide vital knowledge about a subject, its incorporation into a machine learning model is often difficult due to the lack of a suitable method. Consequentially, many researchers rely on straightforward statistical techniques, even when thorough domain knowledge is available. We suggest that machine learning models have the potential to act as powerful tools for absorbing and processing knowledge, and we outline a step-by-step framework for integrating domain expertise using Bayesian methods. We illustrate this approach with concrete examples from the pharmaceutical and environmental fields. We demonstrate how bayesian learning can help exploit structural information present in a subject, even when data is scarce, as shown with a biographical study. We also conducted an experiment showing how bayesian learning can identify and categorize complex carbonation processes. Finally, we developed an application for predicting side effects of new drugs based on their chemical structure and related medical information, which is often known as the JChem for Java project's gRXN network. Our work highlights the importance of training multiple experts, whether human or machine, to address pressing real-world issues. We hope that our comprehensive blueprint will inspire a more unified strategy for integrating domain knowledge and develop more sophisticated models. We intend for this guide to be a starting point rather than a complete manual, and we welcome contributions and further research from the community to enhance the quality and usefulness of machine learning models built on domain knowledge. You can access the related code at https://github.com/fergusondomainblueprint. Additionally, an updated version of this paper, including additional files, is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.11233. Creating a COVID-19 diagnosis tool based on chest CT scans requires collecting numerous, time-consuming, and costly annotations. This research proposes an innovative approach to develop an unbiased and generalizable model for localizing and segmenting COVID-19 lesions using weakly supervised learning techniques. Our method incorporates a combined objective function that optimizes both semi-supervised segmentation and active learning-based annotation correction. This approach enables the accurate propagation of annotated information and enhances unsupervised segmentation quality. Furthermore, an adaptive selection mechanism is designed to optimize the active learning process by identifying the most informative, previously unannotated pixels. This mechanism utilizes pixel classification and region-of-interest scoring to determine the most relevant regions for annotation. When put into action, the model achieves superior performance in unbiased lesion localization and segmentation, and exhibits greater robustness to variations in data quality and distribution compared to a benchmark model. Additionally, the results indicate that the model performs on par with a fully supervised approach when provided with access to a small set of high-quality annotations. As such, it has the potential to contribute to the current research efforts on combating the COVID-19 pandemic. The associated COVID-19 dataset is available for download at https://github.com/Iz4ever/Open-Source-Dataset-COVID19. Identifying vertebrae in CT scans is essential for assessment and diagnosis in conditions such as spinal deformities and osteoporosis. A method has been developed for automatically locating and identifying vertebrae in spinal CT scans. The approach utilizes a rectification technique to align the spine in the image, followed by a template matching technique that incorporates anatomical constraints to identify each vertebra. Evaluation showed that the method successfully localized 100% of vertebrae and accurately identified 100% of vertebrae in a standard dataset, while also demonstrating high levels of reproducibility. Furthermore, the method's accuracy was comparable to that of human observers in terms of centimeter and millimeter accuracy. A comprehensive evaluation was also conducted using a unique dataset of 4000 scans, spanning multiple demographics and spinal conditions, as part of a research challenge. A combination of the method with additional processing steps was found to be effective in determining the height, shape, and position of vertebrae. Through statistical analysis, the method was shown to be sensitive to anatomical spine deformities, while also detecting signs of osteoporotic compression fractures. A standalone software package and source code are available for the method, which has been successfully applied in clinical research settings. Electrons can transfer into the cavity and quickly collide with vacuum waves of varying frequencies, creating a resonance.
This collision can lead to a temporary balance between the electron's movement and the frequency oscillations within the cavity.
This equilibrium is stabilized by the influence of virtual photons even though the frequency is far off from a stable stationary point.
By examining how the cavity's structure affects this interaction, we demonstrate that it's possible to control the electron's movement faster than it would in a normal scattering process. 
This new regime of interaction opens a door to investigating complex quantum behaviors involving atoms, electrons, and photons in confined spaces. 
The methods we've developed can be applied to understanding how atoms respond to each other within confined spaces and what implications this has for their internal movements. 
Finally, we've outlined possible ways to observe this new interaction in experiments involving ultrafast lasers and scanning electron beams.

Determining depth from a single unknown view of a light field is an intricate problem that becomes even more complex when there's occlusion present. This study moves away from point-based approaches and instead explores how to estimate depth through epipolar plane arrays. Specifically, it adapts a novel end-to-end deep learning approach, initially designed for 4D light field data, for situations when there's limited data in epipolar planes. The new framework, called an occlusion-aware cost builder, uses reference data in multiple directions around an unknown view to estimate depth and considers the occlusion in that view by weighing the importance of each reference view. We also introduce a fully differentiable approach that makes it easier to train this cost builder. To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it is essential to improve performance capabilities. The integration of IEEE 802.11k/v technology offers valuable tools for optimizing home WiFi networks, including detailed network analysis and data transmission statistics. By leveraging these measures, it becomes possible to identify and mitigate problems such as overlapping network signals and inefficient resource allocation. A new method, based on IEEE 802.11k/v, is proposed to optimize home WiFi networks by assigning each device to the most suitable access point or extender, taking into account signal quality and remaining channel capacity. Experimental results demonstrate that in a real-world home network setting, this method can effectively reduce signal interference and improve device data transmission rates. Furthermore, it is shown that in a dynamic environment with moving devices, this method can adaptively select the most suitable access points or extenders, thus maintaining optimal network performance. All necessary implementation details to integrate this method into existing home WiFi networks are provided.
